bivy.water: Goat Creek and its tributaries run through the basin and are reliable well into the season; treat everything
bivy.permit: Goat Rocks Wilderness permit, free and self-issued from the box at the trailhead — no reservation and no fee. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at Berry Patch or the Snowgrass trailhead. CAMPING WITHIN SNOWGRASS FLAT ITSELF IS PROHIBITED, along with camping within 100 feet of the Pacific Crest Trail and within 100 feet of any lake. Camp only in pre-existing sites.
bivy.notes: The standard base for Old Snowy and Ives Peak, and for the West Route on Gilbert. The name misleads: the flat proper is a closed meadow and the legal camping is in the timber and on the benches a little below it, around 6,000 to 6,300 feet, roughly three to four miles from the road. From here Old Snowy is a walk-up on a spur off the crest, Ives is a scree-and-ridge scramble off the col between the two, and Gilbert is a long committing day traversing goat ledges across Cispus Basin at 7,400 to 7,600 feet before the southwest slope. This is the most heavily used corner of the wilderness and the parking fills on weekdays, so arriving Friday evening for a Saturday climb is a poor plan. The meadows hold snow into July in a normal year, which is pleasant for the scrambles and awkward for finding a dry pitch.

bivy.name: Goat Lake basin
bivy.capacity: A modest number of established sites scattered back from the shore; the closest ground to the water is off limits, which cuts the usable count sharply
bivy.water: The lake, plus outlet streams; the lake can stay partly frozen into midsummer, in which case take water from the outlet
bivy.permit: Same free self-issued wilderness permit and Northwest Forest Pass as the rest of this trailhead. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED within a quarter mile of the lake shore, so bring a stove and do not plan on a fire. The 100-foot setback from lakes applies here and is actively enforced by the condition of the ground.
bivy.notes: The other basin camp on this side, reached by the loop that swings north from the Snowgrass trail, and a reasonable alternative when the Snowgrass sites are taken. It sits under Old Snowy's western flank and is slightly further from the crest than Snowgrass, which costs you distance on a summit morning but buys a quieter night. The basin is a cirque and holds snow late, so early-season parties frequently find the lake iced and the campsites buried — the trade for a genuinely alpine setting. Vegetation here is fragile and slow-growing, which is why the existing sites are the only acceptable ones.

bivy.name: Dana Yelverton Shelter site
bivy.capacity: A handful of small tents on the crest at best; there is no shelter left to sleep in and the ground is broken rock
bivy.water: None. Snow patches persist nearby into midsummer and can be melted, but from late summer this is a dry camp and water must be carried up from the basin
bivy.permit: Free self-issued Goat Rocks Wilderness permit. CAMPFIRES ARE SPECIFICALLY PROHIBITED at this location by wilderness regulation, and the 100-foot setback from the Pacific Crest Trail applies — the trail passes right through, so a legal pitch here takes some walking.
bivy.notes: A named point on the crest just below Old Snowy, where a stone shelter once stood and where a hiker died in a summer blizzard in the early 1960s. The shelter is now a scatter of rubble and offers no protection whatsoever, so treat the name as a map label rather than a resource. Its value is position: it is the highest place on this side you can legally sleep, which shortens a summit morning on Old Snowy to almost nothing and puts Ives within an easy pre-dawn traverse. The cost is that it is fully exposed at the high point of the Pacific Crest Trail in Washington, with no water, no wind shelter and no retreat that is not a long descent. The history is the warning: weather arrives here fast and out of season.

bivy.name: Chambers Lake Campground
bivy.capacity: A small forested campground with basic single and double sites; first come, first served
bivy.water: No potable water on site — bring your own or filter from the lake. Vault toilets are provided
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed for the campground itself, since it sits outside the boundary. A modest per-night fee has been charged in some seasons and waived in others, so carry cash and check the board on arrival. A Northwest Forest Pass is still required at Berry Patch and the Snowgrass trailhead a short distance up the road.
bivy.notes: The obvious drive-in base for the Goat Rocks crest, under a mile from both the Berry Patch and Snowgrass trailheads, so you can sleep at the car and be walking at first light without the four-mile carry to Snowgrass. That makes it the right choice for a car-to-car attempt on Old Snowy, and a sensible staging night before shouldering a pack for Ives or Gilbert. It is heavily timbered and low, so there is no view and no acclimatisation value, and the approach roads are long gravel with washboard — allow more driving time than the mileage suggests. Snow closes the access road well into spring, which is the practical limit on early-season attempts from this side.

bivy.name: Conrad Meadows and Surprise Lake, South Fork Tieton
bivy.capacity: Primitive dispersed and stock camping in the broad meadows at the road end, and established backcountry sites at Surprise Lake several miles up the loop; no reservations and no numbered sites
bivy.water: The South Fork Tieton and its tributaries throughout, and the lake itself higher up; abundant by the standards of the range's east side but still to be treated
bivy.permit: Free self-issued wilderness permit at the trailhead board once you cross into the wilderness. Camping is prohibited within 100 feet of lakes. Note this trailhead sits on the drier eastern forest rather than the Gifford Pinchot side, so confirm which parking pass the board is asking for before leaving the car. Heavy stock use means the meadows are shared with horse parties.
bivy.notes: This is the correct side of the range for Gilbert Peak's Conrad Glacier and Meade Glacier routes, and there is no sensible way to reach either from the Snowgrass trailheads — the two approaches are separated by the whole crest. From the road end the trail runs level through meadows for around four miles before the loop divides, and the northern fork leads toward Surprise Lake and eventually the benches, waterfall and Barren Lake below the Conrad Glacier. Most parties camp once in the basin and climb from there, since the glacier and the traverse across the Meade to Gilbert's south ridge make for a long day on their own. The meadows at the road end are a legitimate first night if you arrive late, but they are low, buggy in early summer and a long way from anything. This side is far quieter than Snowgrass, and the corresponding cost is a much longer approach and much less traffic if something goes wrong.

bivy.name: Climbers Bivouac
bivy.capacity: Around fourteen small primitive tent sites, close together, first come and first served only; motorhomes and trailers are directed elsewhere
bivy.water: None. There is no water at the trailhead, so carry everything you need for the night and for the climb. Pit toilets are provided
bivy.permit: Camping itself is free, but the parking requires a Northwest Forest Pass, an Interagency pass, or a small day fee. SEPARATELY AND UNAVOIDABLY, a climbing permit is required year round for anyone going above 4,800 feet on the mountain, and camping above 4,800 feet is prohibited outright. From April 1 to October 31 that permit carries a daily quota and a per-climber fee of about twenty dollars: 350 climbers a day from April 1 to May 14, then only 110 a day from May 15 through October 31. Permits are sold first come, first served with no lottery, released a month at a time on the first day of the preceding month at seven in the morning Pacific time, and the summer dates sell out within minutes of release. From November 1 to March 31 the permit is free and self-issued at the trailhead with no quota. Blue bags are mandatory for all human waste above the tree line and are stocked at the trailhead kiosk.
bivy.notes: The summer roadhead for Monitor Ridge, and effectively the only place to sleep close to that route, since the mountain above 4,800 feet is closed to camping. It is a rough clearing in second-growth timber at the end of a Forest Service road, with tent pads and fire rings but nothing else, and the sites are small and packed in. The value is purely positional: the summit trail leaves from here and a night at the trailhead turns a long day into a manageable one. Plan the permit before the campsite, because the permit is the real constraint — the quota tightens sharply in mid-May, and the whole summer sells on release day. Arrive with your blue bag and use it; there is a composting toilet where the trail meets the tree line, and above that there is nothing at all.

bivy.name: Marble Mountain Sno-Park
bivy.capacity: Two large plowed lots plus adjacent forest; winter parties routinely pitch tents in and beside the lots, so capacity is generous and informal rather than defined
bivy.water: None liquid in winter — melt snow, and carry water in the shoulder seasons. Two vault toilets are provided, and a warming hut is open through the winter months
bivy.permit: A Washington Sno-Park permit is required from December 1 to March 31, and this is a non-motorised area. The Mount St. Helens climbing permit is still required for anyone above 4,800 feet, but through the winter window it is free, self-issued at the trailhead and unlimited — the single easiest time of year to climb this mountain from a paperwork point of view. The 4,800-foot camping prohibition applies in winter exactly as it does in summer.
bivy.notes: The winter and shoulder-season staging point, and the start of the Worm Flows route when the road to Climbers Bivouac is under snow. It is lower than the summer trailhead, so Worm Flows carries a bigger day at roughly 5,700 feet of gain, which is the main argument for sleeping here rather than driving in the dark. Camping in a plowed parking lot is not scenic and it works: the lots are large, the toilets are open and the warming hut takes the edge off a cold morning. Parties commonly move up to camp on the snow around the Chocolate Falls area on the way, which stays below the 4,800-foot line if you site it carefully — check your altimeter rather than guessing, because that boundary is a legal one. Avalanche conditions on the Worm Flows gullies, not the permit, are the season's real gate.

bivy.name: Wallace Creek basin ridge camp
bivy.capacity: Two or three tents on the last flat ground beside the highest trees; more parties than that and people are pitching on open snow
bivy.water: Running water is unreliable at this height. In spring, when the peak is in condition, you melt snow, which is what nearly every party does. Later in the year expect to carry from the tarns at the saddle below
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, inside the Mount Baker Wilderness, whose boundary you cross on the way up into the basin. No overnight wilderness permit is required and none is issued for this area. Party size is capped at twelve. A Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass covers parking at the road end. This is national forest, not national park, so no park backcountry permit applies and none can be obtained for it. Stoves rather than fires, and pack out everything including waste on snow
bivy.notes: This is the established high camp for Lincoln and the one nearly every ascent uses. It sits on the ridge overlooking the Wallace Creek basin, right at the last stand of trees, with the Black Buttes and the summit block in view above. Reaching it means walking the road to about the seventh switchback, picking up the old track that leads toward Rankin Creek, scrambling into the basin, passing east Rankin Lake, then climbing mellow snow north to the saddle near 5,480 ft and east up the basin below Seward to the ridge. From here the X Couloir on the southwest face and the north ridge are both single-push summit days, and both are long, steep, exposed snow and ice, which is why the camp is high. The peak is in condition in spring, when fresh snow has mostly stopped falling but nights are still cold enough to hold the snow, ice and rock together; by high summer the face becomes loose and dangerous. Expect the trees to be buried and the ground to be snow. Nothing here is sheltered from weather coming off Baker.

bivy.name: East Rankin Lake
bivy.capacity: Two or three tents around the lake basin on snow or, late in the year, on gravel and heather away from the shore
bivy.water: The lake, once it has melted out. In the spring climbing season it is frozen and buried, so plan on melting snow
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest and Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit required, twelve-person party limit, recreation pass for the vehicle at the road end. No campfires above treeline; use a stove. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and keep off the heather when it is out
bivy.notes: The lower of the two natural stopping places on the approach, in the Rankin Creek basin below the saddle. It is the sensible camp for a party that started late, that is walking extra road miles because of the washout, or that wants an easier carry on day one and a longer summit day on day two. From here the route continues north on easy-angled snow to the small saddle and then east into the upper basin, so nothing is wasted. The cost is close to a thousand feet of climbing left over for summit morning on a route where the difficulties start high. In spring the lake is a flat white plain and easy to camp on; later in the season the basin brushes up and the ground around the water is soggy.

bivy.name: Saddle tarns above Rankin Creek
bivy.capacity: One or two tents on the flats beside the small lakes; informal ground with no established site
bivy.water: Two small tarns sit right at the saddle. They are usually still under snow through the spring climbing season, so treat them as a summer source and otherwise melt snow
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit, twelve-person limit, recreation pass at the road end. Stove only
bivy.notes: The small saddle north of the Rankin basin, with a pair of tarns beside it, sitting between east Rankin Lake and the climb east into the upper basin below Seward. It is a stopgap rather than a destination: only a few hundred feet above the lake and still well short of the ridge camp, so it is chosen mostly by parties caught by weather or darkness on the way up. It is a windy notch, which is worth knowing before you commit to it in a storm. The one thing it does well is mark the point where the approach turns from valley travel to open alpine snow, so it is a useful place to re-assess conditions before carrying a heavy load higher.

bivy.name: Middle Fork Nooksack road switchbacks
bivy.capacity: Roadside pullouts at the lower switchbacks take a couple of vehicles each; there are no built sites, no tables and no toilets
bivy.water: Creeks cross and run down the road in spring, and Rankin Creek is nearby. Treat anything you take
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, outside the wilderness boundary at this elevation. Dispersed roadside camping, no permit, no reservation. Check the current fire restrictions before lighting anything and expect fires to be banned outright in dry spells; a stove is the safe assumption. Pack out all rubbish
bivy.notes: Sleeping at the vehicle the night before is the normal way to start this climb, because the approach is long and parties want to be walking in the dark. The switchbacks above the road's lower section give rough pullouts around 2,650 to 3,420 ft depending on how far the surface lets you drive; past the first switchback the brush closes in and the potholes get serious, and a small car will not make it far. With the road currently barriered at milepost 7 the practical bivouac is wherever the closure puts you, and the Rankin Creek switchbacks are then a long walk or bike ride away — a bicycle to the closure point is worth considering. No elevation is given here because the usable spot depends entirely on how far up the road is open in a given season, which changes.

bivy.name: Toe of the Fryingpan Glacier
bivy.capacity: A small number of parties on moraine and snow at the glacier's lower edge; informal, and the usable ground shifts as the ice recedes

bivy.name: Whitman Glacier notch camp
bivy.capacity: Two or three tents in the gap, dug into snow; very limited and fully exposed
bivy.water: Snow only. No running water at this elevation — carry all fuel for the bivouac and for summit day
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone wilderness permit, plus the climbing cost-recovery fee, which is mandatory here in every sense. Registration for the climb is completed in person at a wilderness information center before you start, and the climbing rangers' account of current glacier and rockfall conditions is worth treating as part of the plan rather than a formality. Blue bags for all waste.
bivy.notes: The highest of the three camps, in the prominent gap on the crest between the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers, just under the base of the peak itself. Sound judgement is to camp high only if the freezing level is low enough to keep the mountain frozen overnight.

bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — a developed Forest Service campground outside the park boundary, reservable through the federal booking system. It sits outside the national park, which means it is not subject to the park entrance fee or to any timed-entry reservation the park may be operating for its corridors; you pay and queue for those the following morning on the way in. bivy.name: Middle Fork Campground
bivy.capacity: About 36 tent and trailer units plus a pair of group sites, no hookups, all reservable. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.water: Potable water is provided from a solar-pumped system, but it has failed for stretches in recent seasons and been shut off mid-summer. Carry enough for the first night rather than counting on the tap. The river runs alongside the campground year-round and can be filtered.
bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, booked up to six months ahead through the federal reservation system or by phone; the adjacent day-use parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or a small daily fee. No wilderness permit applies at the campground itself. Forest-wide campfire bans are routine through late summer and one is in force at the time of writing, so confirm before planning a fire. A food storage order applies across the whole forest.
bivy.notes: The only developed drive-in camping on the Middle Fork road, and the practical roadhead base for every peak in this zone. It sits at about road mile twelve, a few minutes below the Middle Fork trailhead, so a party sleeping here is already at the start of the Preacher Mountain approach and within a short drive of the Garfield pull-outs. The road to it is paved the whole way now, which is a recent change and makes this reachable in any car. Season is roughly mid-May to mid-September; outside those months the gate is shut and the valley has no legal developed option at all. Book ahead, because this is the closest forest campground to Seattle and summer weekends fill months in advance. For Mount Teneriffe parties it is the nearest legal camping of any kind, about twenty minutes' drive from that trailhead.

bivy.name: Middle Fork road pull-outs, Taylor River and Dingford Creek
bivy.capacity: Informal gravel pull-outs only, a vehicle or two apiece, nothing signed, levelled or established.
bivy.water: The river and its side creeks are within a few minutes of the road the entire length of the valley and run all year. Treat everything; this is a heavily used corridor.
bivy.permit: This is the field that decides whether you can sleep here at all. A forest order closes dispersed camping along the road from the forest boundary up to the confluence of the Taylor and Middle Fork rivers, and along the Taylor River road out to the Snoqualmie Lake trailhead, including a quarter-mile strip on either side. That closure runs through the end of 2026 and covers essentially every pull-out parties used to use, including the ones nearest the Garfield approaches. Above the confluence, on the upper road toward Dingford Creek, roadside camping is not covered by the order. Trailhead parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or the interagency equivalent.
bivy.notes: Worth reading before driving up with a plan to sleep in the back of the car, because the situation has changed and the change is not obvious on the ground. The lower valley is closed to dispersed camping, so the answer there is the campground or nothing. The Taylor River road is gated at the bridge at the end of the drivable road and its old roadbed is now the trail, so there is no driving in to a quieter spot. The upper road toward Dingford Creek is the one stretch still open to roadside camping, and it is currently cut by a washout at about road mile seventeen that closes vehicle access short of the Dingford Creek trailhead at 1,400 ft. That washout matters well beyond camping: with it in place the Mount Price approach and the Treen Peak path both gain several road miles on foot or bike each way, which turns two long days into overnight trips. Beyond the Dingford Creek trailhead the road has been gated to vehicles for years in any case. Road status in this valley changes year to year, so confirm the current state with the ranger district before committing; a party that discovers the washout at the barricade has lost the day.

bivy.name: Hester Lake and Myrtle Lake basins
bivy.capacity: A few established, flat tent spots at Hester Lake, enough for two or three parties before it feels crowded. Myrtle Lake, at about 3,780 ft and a couple of miles nearer the road, has a smaller number of rougher sites.
bivy.water: Both lakes are reliable all season, and Dingford Creek runs the length of the approach. Filter or treat.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead: fill it in, drop the stub in the box, carry your copy. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group size is capped at twelve people. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this side of the wilderness; both lakes sit just under that line so a fire is technically legal, but the ground is thin and the sites are heavily used, and stoves are the better answer. Seasonal fire bans override all of that and are common by August.
bivy.notes: This is the real base camp for Mount Price, and the only one. The Dingford Creek trail climbs steeply from the trailhead, passes the Myrtle Lake junction at a little over three miles, and reaches Hester Lake at around five and a half; beyond the junction the tread deteriorates noticeably and the crossings multiply. Price rises directly above Hester, and both the Hester Lake Route and the North Route stage out of this basin, so a party camping here is looking at their objective from the tent. Myrtle is the softer option if the day runs out early, but it puts you further from the peak. Snow lingers in these basins into June and the summit slopes hold it later, so July through early October is the window. With the road washout in place the whole trip is several miles longer each way, which pushes this from a fit party's long day firmly into an overnight.

bivy.name: Green Ridge Lake
bivy.capacity: Small informal camp on the benches by the lake, room for a couple of tents. Nothing designated or maintained. Tarns on the ridge above take another tent or two.
bivy.water: The lake is reliable through the summer, and the tarns above hold water into late season most years. Nothing between the road and the lake once the low creeks are behind you, so fill before the steep section.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit where the boundary is crossed, group size capped at twelve. The start is an unsigned roadside pull-out rather than a developed trailhead, so carry a Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle. The lake sits just below the 4,000 ft campfire line and the ridge camps above it are stoves-only regardless; treat the whole area as no-fire in practice.
bivy.notes: The staging point for two of this zone's objectives and the one genuinely useful high camp on the north side of the valley. Treen Peak's Green Ridge approach starts here, and so does the East Peak ridge on the Garfield massif, which is the one part of that mountain with a walking line rather than a climb. Access is a faint unmaintained miners' and fishermen's path leaving the upper road at about 1,350 ft, roughly a mile below the Dingford Creek trailhead, climbing steeply northeast through timber; it is easy to lose in the first thousand feet and the brush is heavy when wet. Above the ridge crest at about 4,700 ft the ground opens into heather and scattered tarns and travel becomes pleasant. For most parties this is a contingency rather than the plan, since Treen goes in a long day when the road is open, but the road washout and the sheer gain from 1,350 ft make an overnight the sensible choice at present, and the ridge camp splits a brutal day into two reasonable ones. Season is July into October; the approach is snow-free early but the brush stays soaking until the summer settles.

bivy.name: Rainy Lake
bivy.capacity: A handful of informal sites around the lake shore. Quiet and rarely busy, since the access path keeps the numbers down.
bivy.water: The lake and Rainy Creek are both reliable through the season. Treat.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit, group limit twelve. Northwest Forest Pass at the Middle Fork trailhead where the approach begins. The lake is just under the 4,000 ft campfire line, but the sites are small and the ground is thin, so use a stove and expect seasonal bans in late summer.
bivy.notes: Sits directly beneath the exposed south face of Preacher Mountain and is the natural base camp for the Standard Scramble. From the Middle Fork trailhead cross the bridge and follow the Pratt connector west to the junction with the unofficial Rainy Creek path, which the Forest Service abandoned years ago; volunteers keep the brush down in places and much of it is flagged, but it is not maintained tread and route-finding is required, particularly in the lower half. Preacher is around eleven miles and five thousand feet of gain from the road when it goes well, so most parties do it car-to-car. Treat this as the contingency for a slow day, wet brush or a late descent, and as the sensible plan for a winter attempt, when Preacher becomes a real snowshoe objective and the daylight will not stretch. The valley floor here is low enough to be open most of the year, but the lake and the ridge above hold snow into June.

bivy.name: Garfield Mountain improvised bivouac
bivy.capacity: Nothing established, and no honest capacity figure to give. Parties sleep where the terrain offers a flat dry patch, a bench in a gully, a ledge system or a heather shoulder, usually one or two people at a time.

Ascents here are commonly described as needing either a bivouac or the very longest days of the year to finish in daylight, and the bivouacs that actually happen are improvised where a party runs out of light rather than chosen in advance. Plan for that rather than around it: carry a bivy kit on any attempt, expect to sleep on rock or in brush, and treat the multi-summit outing in particular as an opportunistic link-up rather than a route with a known camp on it. Substantial rappels separate some of the summits, so retreat is not always the quick option once committed. The one exception is the East Peak, whose ridge is gained from Green Ridge; a party going that way should use the Green Ridge Lake camp above instead of anything on this face. Season here is governed by dry rock and daylight rather than snow: the valley is open most of the year, but the brush stays wet late and June through September is when this goes.

bivy.name: Middle Fork Campground
bivy.capacity: About 36 tent and trailer units plus a pair of group sites, no hookups, all reservable. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.water: Potable water is provided from a solar-pumped system, but it has failed for stretches in recent seasons and been shut off mid-summer. Carry enough for the first night rather than counting on the tap. The river runs alongside the campground year-round and can be filtered.
bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, booked up to six months ahead through the federal reservation system or by phone; the adjacent day-use parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or a small daily fee. No wilderness permit applies at the campground itself. Forest-wide campfire bans are routine through late summer and one is in force at the time of writing, so confirm before planning a fire. A food storage order applies across the whole forest.
bivy.notes: The only developed drive-in camping on the Middle Fork road, and the practical roadhead base for every peak in this zone. It sits at about road mile twelve, a few minutes below the Middle Fork trailhead, so a party sleeping here is already at the start of the Preacher Mountain approach and within a short drive of the Garfield pull-outs. The road to it is paved the whole way now, which is a recent change and makes this reachable in any car. bivy.name: Middle Fork road pull-outs, Taylor River and Dingford Creek
bivy.capacity: Informal gravel pull-outs only, a vehicle or two apiece, nothing signed, levelled or established.
bivy.water: The river and its side creeks are within a few minutes of the road the entire length of the valley and run all year. Treat everything; this is a heavily used corridor.

Beyond the Dingford Creek trailhead the road has been gated to vehicles for years in any case. bivy.name: Hester Lake and Myrtle Lake basins

Seasonal fire bans override all of that and are common by August.

bivy.name: Green Ridge Lake

Substantial rappels separate some of the summits, so retreat is not always the quick option once committed. The one exception is the East Peak, whose ridge is gained from Green Ridge; a party going that way should use the Green Ridge Lake camp above instead of anything on this face. Season here is governed by dry rock and daylight rather than snow: the valley is open most of the year, but the brush stays wet late and June through September is when this goes.

bivy.name: Mount Teneriffe and the Mount Si conservation area, no overnight
bivy.capacity: None. Camping is prohibited across the entire conservation area, at any elevation, so there is no legal overnight option anywhere on this mountain.
bivy.water: The falls and the creeks crossed low on the trail run most of the year and are the last certain water. There is nothing on the upper mountain and nothing on the Kamikaze line at all. Carry what you need for the day.
bivy.permit: A Washington Discover Pass is required in every vehicle at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass is not valid here, which is the commonest mistake parties make arriving from the national forest roads further up the valley, and the fines are real. Camping and campfires are both prohibited, group size is capped at twelve, and the trails are hiking-only.
bivy.notes: Recorded because it is the honest answer rather than a place to sleep. Mount Teneriffe is state conservation land at the very front of the range, reached from its own trailhead at the end of the Mount Si road and not from any of the Middle Fork trailheads that serve the other peaks here, so it has a different land manager, a different pass and different rules. Both the standard trail and the Kamikaze scramble up the southwest ridge are done car-to-car in a day by everyone who climbs them, and there is no camp on the mountain and nothing legal near the trailhead. A party that wants to start from a tent has to drop back to the valley, where the Middle Fork Campground is the nearest developed option, about twenty minutes' drive up the road system. The compensation is season: the lower mountain is snow-free most of the year and this is a genuine winter and shoulder-season objective, though the steep upper section of the Kamikaze line becomes icy and unpleasant once the freeze sets in and the standard trail is the safer choice then.

bivy.name: Middle Fork Campground
bivy.capacity: About 36 tent and trailer units plus a pair of group sites, no hookups, all reservable. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.water: Potable water is provided from a solar-pumped system, but it has failed for stretches in recent seasons and been shut off mid-summer. Carry enough for the first night rather than counting on the tap. The river runs alongside the campground year-round and can be filtered.
bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, booked up to six months ahead through the federal reservation system or by phone; the adjacent day-use parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or a small daily fee. No wilderness permit applies at the campground itself. Forest-wide campfire bans are routine through late summer and one is in force at the time of writing, so confirm before planning a fire. A food storage order applies across the whole forest.
bivy.notes: The only developed drive-in camping on the Middle Fork road, and the practical roadhead base for every peak in this zone. It sits at about road mile twelve, a few minutes below the Middle Fork trailhead, so a party sleeping here is already at the start of the Preacher Mountain approach and within a short drive of the Garfield pull-outs. The road to it is paved the whole way now, which is a recent change and makes this reachable in any car. Season is roughly mid-May to mid-September; outside those months the gate is shut and the valley has no legal developed option at all. Book ahead, because this is the closest forest campground to Seattle and summer weekends fill months in advance. For Mount Teneriffe parties it is the nearest legal camping of any kind, about twenty minutes' drive from that trailhead.

bivy.name: Middle Fork road pull-outs, Taylor River and Dingford Creek
bivy.capacity: Informal gravel pull-outs only, a vehicle or two apiece, nothing signed, levelled or established.
bivy.water: The river and its side creeks are within a few minutes of the road the entire length of the valley and run all year. Treat everything; this is a heavily used corridor.
bivy.permit: This is the field that decides whether you can sleep here at all. A forest order closes dispersed camping along the road from the forest boundary up to the confluence of the Taylor and Middle Fork rivers, and along the Taylor River road out to the Snoqualmie Lake trailhead, including a quarter-mile strip on either side. That closure runs through the end of 2026 and covers essentially every pull-out parties used to use, including the ones nearest the Garfield approaches. Above the confluence, on the upper road toward Dingford Creek, roadside camping is not covered by the order. Trailhead parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or the interagency equivalent.
bivy.notes: Worth reading before driving up with a plan to sleep in the back of the car, because the situation has changed and the change is not obvious on the ground. The lower valley is closed to dispersed camping, so the answer there is the campground or nothing. The Taylor River road is gated at the bridge at the end of the drivable road and its old roadbed is now the trail, so there is no driving in to a quieter spot. The upper road toward Dingford Creek is the one stretch still open to roadside camping, and it is currently cut by a washout at about road mile seventeen that closes vehicle access short of the Dingford Creek trailhead at 1,400 ft. That washout matters well beyond camping: with it in place the Mount Price approach and the Treen Peak path both gain several road miles on foot or bike each way, which turns two long days into overnight trips. Beyond the Dingford Creek trailhead the road has been gated to vehicles for years in any case. Road status in this valley changes year to year, so confirm the current state with the ranger district before committing; a party that discovers the washout at the barricade has lost the day.

bivy.name: Hester Lake and Myrtle Lake basins
bivy.capacity: A few established, flat tent spots at Hester Lake, enough for two or three parties before it feels crowded. Myrtle Lake, at about 3,780 ft and a couple of miles nearer the road, has a smaller number of rougher sites.
bivy.water: Both lakes are reliable all season, and Dingford Creek runs the length of the approach. Filter or treat.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead: fill it in, drop the stub in the box, carry your copy. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group size is capped at twelve people. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this side of the wilderness; both lakes sit just under that line so a fire is technically legal, but the ground is thin and the sites are heavily used, and stoves are the better answer. Seasonal fire bans override all of that and are common by August.
bivy.notes: This is the real base camp for Mount Price, and the only one. The Dingford Creek trail climbs steeply from the trailhead, passes the Myrtle Lake junction at a little over three miles, and reaches Hester Lake at around five and a half; beyond the junction the tread deteriorates noticeably and the crossings multiply. Price rises directly above Hester, and both the Hester Lake Route and the North Route stage out of this basin, so a party camping here is looking at their objective from the tent. Myrtle is the softer option if the day runs out early, but it puts you further from the peak. Snow lingers in these basins into June and the summit slopes hold it later, so July through early October is the window. With the road washout in place the whole trip is several miles longer each way, which pushes this from a fit party's long day firmly into an overnight.

bivy.name: Green Ridge Lake
bivy.capacity: Small informal camp on the benches by the lake, room for a couple of tents. Nothing designated or maintained. Tarns on the ridge above take another tent or two.
bivy.water: The lake is reliable through the summer, and the tarns above hold water into late season most years. Nothing between the road and the lake once the low creeks are behind you, so fill before the steep section.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit where the boundary is crossed, group size capped at twelve. The start is an unsigned roadside pull-out rather than a developed trailhead, so carry a Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle. The lake sits just below the 4,000 ft campfire line and the ridge camps above it are stoves-only regardless; treat the whole area as no-fire in practice.
bivy.notes: The staging point for two of this zone's objectives and the one genuinely useful high camp on the north side of the valley. Treen Peak's Green Ridge approach starts here, and so does the East Peak ridge on the Garfield massif, which is the one part of that mountain with a walking line rather than a climb. Access is a faint unmaintained miners' and fishermen's path leaving the upper road at about 1,350 ft, roughly a mile below the Dingford Creek trailhead, climbing steeply northeast through timber; it is easy to lose in the first thousand feet and the brush is heavy when wet. Above the ridge crest at about 4,700 ft the ground opens into heather and scattered tarns and travel becomes pleasant. For most parties this is a contingency rather than the plan, since Treen goes in a long day when the road is open, but the road washout and the sheer gain from 1,350 ft make an overnight the sensible choice at present, and the ridge camp splits a brutal day into two reasonable ones. Season is July into October; the approach is snow-free early but the brush stays soaking until the summer settles.

bivy.name: Rainy Lake
bivy.capacity: A handful of informal sites around the lake shore. Quiet and rarely busy, since the access path keeps the numbers down.
bivy.water: The lake and Rainy Creek are both reliable through the season. Treat.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit, group limit twelve. Northwest Forest Pass at the Middle Fork trailhead where the approach begins. The lake is just under the 4,000 ft campfire line, but the sites are small and the ground is thin, so use a stove and expect seasonal bans in late summer.
bivy.notes: Sits directly beneath the exposed south face of Preacher Mountain and is the natural base camp for the Standard Scramble. From the Middle Fork trailhead cross the bridge and follow the Pratt connector west to the junction with the unofficial Rainy Creek path, which the Forest Service abandoned years ago; volunteers keep the brush down in places and much of it is flagged, but it is not maintained tread and route-finding is required, particularly in the lower half. Preacher is around eleven miles and five thousand feet of gain from the road when it goes well, so most parties do it car-to-car. Treat this as the contingency for a slow day, wet brush or a late descent, and as the sensible plan for a winter attempt, when Preacher becomes a real snowshoe objective and the daylight will not stretch. The valley floor here is low enough to be open most of the year, but the lake and the ridge above hold snow into June.

bivy.name: Garfield Mountain improvised bivouac
bivy.capacity: Nothing established, and no honest capacity figure to give. Parties sleep where the terrain offers a flat dry patch, a bench in a gully, a ledge system or a heather shoulder, usually one or two people at a time.
bivy.water: Nothing reliable and nothing to plan around. The gullies run in spring and after rain and are dry by late summer, and there is no snow to melt on this mountain in season. Carry water for the whole push and know where the last certain source below you was.
bivy.permit: No permit for a bivouac on the mountain beyond the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit if your line crosses the boundary, plus a Northwest Forest Pass at whichever pull-out you start from. Note that sleeping at the car is not an option here: the pull-outs at the base of Garfield fall inside the lower-valley dispersed camping closure.
bivy.notes: The honest answer for Garfield is that there is no camp, and inventing one would do a party more harm than saying so. It is a low mountain carrying enormous relief straight out of the valley floor, and every documented line begins with steep unmaintained bushwhacking and long rock gullies before any climbing starts. There are no trails, no signs and no established approach; you leave the road at a pull-out and go up. bivy.name: Three Fingers Lookout, south summit
bivy.capacity: First come, first served, and small. A single sleeping platform takes two comfortably; the floor absorbs another two or three on pads, and parties have squeezed six to eight in at the cost of everyone's night. Treat four as the realistic number and anything above six as an emergency. THERE IS NOWHERE TO PITCH A TENT OUTSIDE — the cabin occupies the whole blasted summit block, so a full lookout means descending.
bivy.water: None at the lookout. The last dependable water is the tarns and runnels around Goat Flats and the snowmelt near the gap below; above that you are melting snow off the glacier or carrying it. Plan on hauling several litres per person up the final stretch and expect to melt if you arrive late in a dry summer.
bivy.permit: No permit and no reservation, and none is available — it cannot be booked. Inside the Boulder River Wilderness, which requires no self-issue permit to camp. A federal recreation pass is the parking requirement at forest trailheads on this side. Campfires are prohibited the whole way from the lake below up to the peak, and there is nothing to burn at the top anyway. The cabin is volunteer-maintained: leave it swept, close the shutters and the door properly against weather and rodents, pack out every scrap including food waste, and do not take or move anything belonging to it. If it has been closed for repair, stay out.
bivy.notes: This is the reason to come here overnight and it is genuinely one of the few summit cabins in the state a climbing party can sleep in. It sits on the southernmost of the three summits, on ground that was blasted flat to seat it, and the final approach to the door is a set of steep wooden ladders bolted against the cliff — vertical, exposed, and not somewhere to be carrying a loose pack or moving in the dark. Getting to them means crossing the glacier on the peak's north side above the gap, which is a real crossing rather than a snowfield walk: axe and crampons all year, a rope and the ability to use it, and late in the season a moat between ice and rock that some parties follow instead, when they can find its entrance. It has been rebuilt and repaired repeatedly by volunteers over the decades, most recently in the structure itself, so it is sound but spartan — bare boards, shutters, no stove worth relying on, no facilities. Coming as a climbing party rather than a hiking one, the sensible plan is to camp lower and go up light, because a full lookout at nine at night with the ladders behind you is a bad position.

bivy.name: Tin Can Gap high camp
bivy.capacity: A few small pitches on rock and snow at and just below the gap; one or two parties, not a group site
bivy.water: Snowmelt only for most of the season, and nothing at all once the snow around the gap has gone. Assume you are melting or carrying from Goat Flats.
bivy.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no camping permit required. Federal recreation pass to park. Campfires prohibited on this whole stretch of trail; there is no fuel here regardless.
bivy.notes: The last flat ground before the glacier, roughly a mile short of the lookout, and the correct camp for a party that wants the summit block early and cold rather than soft. The maintained trail effectively ends here, so everything above is a bootpath, snow and the ladders. Its value is that it puts the glacier crossing and the ladders in the first hour of the day, when the snow is still firm — a real advantage over starting from the meadows two miles back. The cost is exposure: it is a gap, it catches weather, and there is nothing sheltering about it. Camp on rock or snow rather than the thin vegetation, and take a hard look at whether the crossing above is in condition before committing to a camp that only makes sense if you go up.

bivy.name: Goat Flats
bivy.capacity: The main camping area on this approach — several established pockets spread through the meadows and around the tarns. It absorbs a fair number of parties but is genuinely crowded on summer and autumn weekends, and it is the overflow when the lookout is full.
bivy.water: Reliable through most of the season from the tarns and small streams in the meadows, though the standing water is shallow and warms up late in summer. Treat everything. Later in a dry year the tarns shrink and the better water is the running melt above the flats.
bivy.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no camping permit. Federal recreation pass at the trailhead. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED in the Goat Flats area and along this trail generally. Bears work this basin, so hard-sided or hung food storage is expected rather than optional.
bivy.notes: Open subalpine meadow about two miles beyond the lake, and the default base for anything on Three Fingers — the lookout, the middle summit, or a look at the south face. From here the gap and the glacier are within a straightforward morning. It is also the honest fallback for a party that walked up hoping for a bunk in the lookout and found it occupied: about two miles back down from the ladders, which is a long but manageable retreat with headlamps. The meadow soil is thin and heavily used, so pitch on the bare established spots and not on fresh turf. Snow lies here well into summer and the meadows are boggy for weeks after it goes.

bivy.name: Saddle Lake
bivy.capacity: Small — a handful of spots in the timber and meadow near the lake, plus an old volunteer-built shelter at the meadow edge that should be treated as rough emergency cover rather than accommodation
bivy.water: The lake, which is dependable all season and needs treating. This is the last easy water before the meadows above.
bivy.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no camping permit. CAMPING IS PROHIBITED within 200 feet of the shoreline, so the lakeside spots that look obvious are not all legal. Campfires are prohibited within 200 feet of the lake and along the trail above it.
bivy.notes: About two and a half miles in from the road end, in dense timber, and low enough that it is a contingency rather than a plan for anyone climbing. It matters for two reasons. First, the road: the Tupso Pass road has a long washout history and has at times been cut miles short of the trailhead, leaving parties to walk or bike the road grade — when that is the situation the lake is as far as many get on day one. Second, it is where a party that started late, or turned around at the gap in bad conditions, can stop without pushing all the way out. Do not plan a Three Fingers climb from here; it is too low and too far. Bugs are heavy in early summer.

bivy.name: Whitehorse high camp, benches near Lone Tree Pass
bivy.capacity: Informal — a flat sheltered meadow just past the pass takes a couple of tents, with smaller pockets on benches nearby and more ground on the traverse east toward the small lake below the pass. One or two parties.
bivy.water: Snowmelt in season and the small tarn below the pass on the traverse east; both are seasonal. By late summer this side dries out and there may be nothing, so carry up or plan to melt. There is no water on the trail below.
bivy.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no permit to camp, no quota, no self-issue box. No fee at the trailhead, which is unusual for this area and reflects how minimal the parking is. Fires are a bad idea on this ground and are commonly banned outright in late summer.
bivy.notes: This is the high camp for the Northwest Shoulder, and most parties who do not intend a twelve-to-sixteen hour car-to-car day use it. The route is around 6,000 to 7,000 feet of gain from a low trailhead and the lower trail is notoriously steep and brushy, so splitting it at the pass converts a punishing single day into two reasonable ones and puts the glacier and the exposed summit scrambling in the morning. The sheltered meadow just beyond the pass is the pick — trees break the wind and it looks straight at the summit. Everything about this approach depends on the Mine Road out of the highway west of Darrington: it is rough, narrow, overgrown enough to scratch a vehicle, and has had bridge and washout closures that push the start well down the hill and add road walking. Confirm how far you can drive before you plan the day. Early season with snow cover over the brush is much the better time; by late summer the glacier above develops crevasses and a large bergschrund and the brush below is at its worst.

bivy.name: Whitehorse Community Park campground, Darrington
bivy.capacity: A developed county campground with tent and equestrian sites on a large park property; nightly fee
bivy.water: Developed park water in season; confirm before relying on it outside summer
bivy.permit: COUNTY park, not national forest — a nightly fee applies and no federal or state pass does anything here. Seasonal: closed and winterized through the winter months, roughly mid-autumn to mid-spring, which rules it out for the spring snow season when Whitehorse is actually in condition.
bivy.notes: The nearest developed drive-in base to the Mine Road, sitting just outside Darrington with the mountain itself directly in view, which makes it a useful place to look at conditions on the northwest side the evening before. Its real role is staging: the Niederprum trailhead has room for only a handful of vehicles and nothing else, so sleeping in town and driving up in the small hours is the usual pattern rather than camping at the road end. Because it is county-run its season and fees are set separately from the forest campgrounds and change independently of them. The winter closure is the catch — the best window for the Northwest Shoulder is spring, and the campground may not be open yet.

bivy.name: Big Four north-side staging and base bivouac
bivy.capacity: No established camp of any kind. The picnic area at the trailhead is DAY USE ONLY and camping there is not permitted; parties climbing the north side bivouac informally at the base of the face on the avalanche debris and boulder ground beyond the maintained path.
bivy.water: Creeks draining the face run all season near the base, and the debris field itself is meltwater. Treat everything. There is no developed water at the picnic area.
bivy.permit: Not inside any wilderness — this side of the highway is ordinary national forest with no camping permit requirement. A federal recreation pass is required to park at the picnic area. Fire restrictions are common from midsummer and are frequently forest-wide.
bivy.notes: Big Four is a car-to-car objective by design: the trailhead sits at low elevation barely a mile from the base of a face that rises about 4,000 feet, so the climbing starts almost immediately and there is no approach worth camping to shorten. Parties on the north-side lines, including the long winter couloir routes, typically leave overnight gear at the base and go up and down in a push rather than carrying a bivouac onto the face, which is a considered choice on a wall this active — rockfall and avalanche off it are constant and audible through the night. That same activity is why this entry is a contingency and not a recommendation: sleeping under this face means sleeping under a debris cone that is there because things fall on it. Position any bivouac well out of the runout, not at the toe of the snow. THE ICE CAVES AT THE BASE ARE LETHAL and collapse every year — do not camp near them, on them, or in them, and stay off them entirely. The nearest legal drive-in beds are the developed campgrounds down the paved loop toward Verlot.

bivy.name: Bathtub Lakes basin, east of Mount Pilchuck
bivy.capacity: Informal sites among the small lakes and benches of the basin; a few parties, nothing developed
bivy.water: The lakes and their outlets, dependable through the season and needing treatment. This is a wet basin, which is the whole reason it works as a camp.
bivy.permit: The summit and upper mountain are a STATE CONSERVATION AREA rather than national forest, but this basin and the approach to it are forest land and no camping permit applies. The parking requirement at the trailheads on this mountain is the FEDERAL pass — a state Discover Pass is not valid at them, which catches people out because of the state park name. No fires on the state land above, and fire bans are routine below in late summer.
bivy.notes: This is the only real camp on Pilchuck and it serves the east side rather than the standard route. It is reached from below, from the Bear Lake and Pinnacle Lake trailhead on a spur road off the loop east of Verlot, then up past the lower lake and into the gulch above — a loose, brushy, steep piece of ground with vegetation-pulling and poor rock that is the genuine difficulty of the East Ridge, not the ridge itself. Camping in the basin splits that so the gulch is climbed fresh. It has no bearing on the standard summit trail, which leaves the end of the Mount Pilchuck road on the other side of the mountain and is a straightforward day hike to the restored summit lookout with no camping along it and none needed. Treat this as a plan for the east side and as a contingency for anyone who commits to the gulch late and would rather not descend it in the dark.

bivy.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no camping permit. Federal recreation pass at the trailhead. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED in the Goat Flats area and along this trail generally. Bears work this basin, so hard-sided or hung food storage is expected rather than optional.
bivy.notes: Open subalpine meadow about two miles beyond the lake, and the default base for anything on Three Fingers — the lookout, the middle summit, or a look at the south face. From here the gap and the glacier are within a straightforward morning. It is also the honest fallback for a party that walked up hoping for a bunk in the lookout and found it occupied: about two miles back down from the ladders, which is a long but manageable retreat with headlamps. The meadow soil is thin and heavily used, so pitch on the bare established spots and not on fresh turf. Snow lies here well into summer and the meadows are boggy for weeks after it goes.

bivy.name: Saddle Lake
bivy.capacity: Small — a handful of spots in the timber and meadow near the lake, plus an old volunteer-built shelter at the meadow edge that should be treated as rough emergency cover rather than accommodation
bivy.water: The lake, which is dependable all season and needs treating. This is the last easy water before the meadows above.
bivy.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no camping permit. CAMPING IS PROHIBITED within 200 feet of the shoreline, so the lakeside spots that look obvious are not all legal. Campfires are prohibited within 200 feet of the lake and along the trail above it.
bivy.notes: About two and a half miles in from the road end, in dense timber, and low enough that it is a contingency rather than a plan for anyone climbing. It matters for two reasons. First, the road: the Tupso Pass road has a long washout history and has at times been cut miles short of the trailhead, leaving parties to walk or bike the road grade — when that is the situation the lake is as far as many get on day one. Second, it is where a party that started late, or turned around at the gap in bad conditions, can stop without pushing all the way out. Do not plan a Three Fingers climb from here; it is too low and too far. Bugs are heavy in early summer.

bivy.name: Whitehorse high camp, benches near Lone Tree Pass
bivy.capacity: Informal — a flat sheltered meadow just past the pass takes a couple of tents, with smaller pockets on benches nearby and more ground on the traverse east toward the small lake below the pass. One or two parties.
bivy.water: Snowmelt in season and the small tarn below the pass on the traverse east; both are seasonal. By late summer this side dries out and there may be nothing, so carry up or plan to melt. There is no water on the trail below.
bivy.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no permit to camp, no quota, no self-issue box. No fee at the trailhead, which is unusual for this area and reflects how minimal the parking is. Fires are a bad idea on this ground and are commonly banned outright in late summer.
bivy.notes: This is the high camp for the Northwest Shoulder, and most parties who do not intend a twelve-to-sixteen hour car-to-car day use it. The route is around 6,000 to 7,000 feet of gain from a low trailhead and the lower trail is notoriously steep and brushy, so splitting it at the pass converts a punishing single day into two reasonable ones and puts the glacier and the exposed summit scrambling in the morning. The sheltered meadow just beyond the pass is the pick — trees break the wind and it looks straight at the summit. Everything about this approach depends on the Mine Road out of the highway west of Darrington: it is rough, narrow, overgrown enough to scratch a vehicle, and has had bridge and washout closures that push the start well down the hill and add road walking. Confirm how far you can drive before you plan the day. Early season with snow cover over the brush is much the better time; by late summer the glacier above develops crevasses and a large bergschrund and the brush below is at its worst.

bivy.name: Whitehorse Community Park campground, Darrington
bivy.capacity: A developed county campground with tent and equestrian sites on a large park property; nightly fee
bivy.water: Developed park water in season; confirm before relying on it outside summer
bivy.permit: COUNTY park, not national forest — a nightly fee applies and no federal or state pass does anything here. Seasonal: closed and winterized through the winter months, roughly mid-autumn to mid-spring, which rules it out for the spring snow season when Whitehorse is actually in condition.
bivy.notes: The nearest developed drive-in base to the Mine Road, sitting just outside Darrington with the mountain itself directly in view, which makes it a useful place to look at conditions on the northwest side the evening before. Its real role is staging: the Niederprum trailhead has room for only a handful of vehicles and nothing else, so sleeping in town and driving up in the small hours is the usual pattern rather than camping at the road end. Because it is county-run its season and fees are set separately from the forest campgrounds and change independently of them. The winter closure is the catch — the best window for the Northwest Shoulder is spring, and the campground may not be open yet.

bivy.name: Big Four north-side staging and base bivouac
bivy.capacity: No established camp of any kind. The picnic area at the trailhead is DAY USE ONLY and camping there is not permitted; parties climbing the north side bivouac informally at the base of the face on the avalanche debris and boulder ground beyond the maintained path.
bivy.water: Creeks draining the face run all season near the base, and the debris field itself is meltwater. Treat everything. There is no developed water at the picnic area.
bivy.permit: Not inside any wilderness — this side of the highway is ordinary national forest with no camping permit requirement. A federal recreation pass is required to park at the picnic area. Fire restrictions are common from midsummer and are frequently forest-wide.
bivy.notes: Big Four is a car-to-car objective by design: the trailhead sits at low elevation barely a mile from the base of a face that rises about 4,000 feet, so the climbing starts almost immediately and there is no approach worth camping to shorten. Parties on the north-side lines, including the long winter couloir routes, typically leave overnight gear at the base and go up and down in a push rather than carrying a bivouac onto the face, which is a considered choice on a wall this active — rockfall and avalanche off it are constant and audible through the night. That same activity is why this entry is a contingency and not a recommendation: sleeping under this face means sleeping under a debris cone that is there because things fall on it. Position any bivouac well out of the runout, not at the toe of the snow. THE ICE CAVES AT THE BASE ARE LETHAL and collapse every year — do not camp near them, on them, or in them, and stay off them entirely. The nearest legal drive-in beds are the developed campgrounds down the paved loop toward Verlot.

bivy.name: Bathtub Lakes basin, east of Mount Pilchuck
bivy.capacity: Informal sites among the small lakes and benches of the basin; a few parties, nothing developed
bivy.water: The lakes and their outlets, dependable through the season and needing treatment. This is a wet basin, which is the whole reason it works as a camp.
bivy.permit: The summit and upper mountain are a STATE CONSERVATION AREA rather than national forest, but this basin and the approach to it are forest land and no camping permit applies. The parking requirement at the trailheads on this mountain is the FEDERAL pass — a state Discover Pass is not valid at them, which catches people out because of the state park name. No fires on the state land above, and fire bans are routine below in late summer.
bivy.notes: This is the only real camp on Pilchuck and it serves the east side rather than the standard route. It is reached from below, from the Bear Lake and Pinnacle Lake trailhead on a spur road off the loop east of Verlot, then up past the lower lake and into the gulch above — a loose, brushy, steep piece of ground with vegetation-pulling and poor rock that is the genuine difficulty of the East Ridge, not the ridge itself. Camping in the basin splits that so the gulch is climbed fresh. It has no bearing on the standard summit trail, which leaves the end of the Mount Pilchuck road on the other side of the mountain and is a straightforward day hike to the restored summit lookout with no camping along it and none needed. Treat this as a plan for the east side and as a contingency for anyone who commits to the gulch late and would rather not descend it in the dark.

bivy.name: Rock Lake
bivy.capacity: Several pleasant established sites around the lake, enough for two or three parties; small and it feels small, with no facilities
bivy.water: The lake, and it is the first water of any kind on the Rock Mountain trail — the entire climb from the highway is dry. It holds all season. Treat it, because the shoreline is well used and the basin is small. Fill here for everything you intend to do on the crest, since the next dependable source westward or eastward is Crescent Lake, and the ridge between the two carries nothing.
bivy.permit: None. Nason Ridge sits outside the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, so there is no wilderness permit, no self-issue slip, no quota and no lottery anywhere in this file. The Rock Mountain trailhead has very limited parking and a Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent is the usual requirement there; the Merritt Lake end requires no pass at all, which is an inconsistency worth checking at the board rather than assuming. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet in this national forest, which covers this camp and every other high site here, and summer burn bans are routine on this dry east-side ground.
bivy.notes: The camp for Rock Mountain and the western anchor of the whole crest. The Rock Mountain trail leaves US 2 at about 2,650 feet and is relentless — roughly 3,400 feet in four miles of endless switchbacks on a hot, open, south-facing slope with no water and very little shade, which is the single most quoted complaint about this peak. The lake sits in a basin below the summit ridge, so a party that has ground up the trail can drop packs, camp, and take the northeast ridge and the summit unencumbered. Most people do Rock Mountain in a day; camping here is what you do when the heat has beaten you, when you are starting the Nason Ridge traverse rather than finishing it, or when you want the summit at first light. The alternative approach by the Snowy Creek trail from the forest road on the north side starts higher and climbs less, and it is the kinder line in warm weather, though the road is brushy. Snow lingers on the upper slopes into early summer and the basin holds it later than the trail below. West of the lake, the crest trail toward Crescent Lake has badly eroded steep sidehill sections with little tread left, and that stretch is the crux of moving along this ridge with a pack.

bivy.name: Crescent Lake
bivy.capacity: Lakeside sites for a handful of tents, quieter than Merritt because it takes real effort to reach from either direction; use the existing spots rather than clearing new ground on the vegetation
bivy.water: The lake plus several small running streams in the immediate surroundings, which is unusually generous for this ridge and is exactly why parties fill their bottles here before going up. It is dependable through the season. Everything above the lake is dry, so the four quarts you want for a summit camp or a long crest day come from here.
bivy.permit: None — no wilderness, no permit, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass at the Rock Mountain trailhead; none required at Merritt Lake. No campfires above 5,000 feet, which includes this lake, and expect a total burn ban most of the summer.
bivy.notes: The base camp for both Mount Howard and Mount Mastiff, and the natural halfway house on the crest traverse. It sits on the Nason Ridge trail one and three tenths miles beyond Rock Lake, reached by traversing a loose slope around the intervening ridge and dropping about three hundred feet, or from the other direction three and a half miles west of Merritt Lake. From the lake the south slope route on Howard goes around the northeast side and straight up, skirting trees and slide alder to a rock band that is passed by any of several easy scrambling gullies onto a large bench; from the bench you can go directly up the south flank to Howard's summit or traverse east onto the southeast ridge. Bugs are heavy through June and early July, and the approach from either end holds snow on the north-facing traverses well into summer.

bivy.name: Merritt Lake

Anyone continuing toward Alpine Lookout is carrying every drop from this shore. Treat it; the camp is heavily used.
bivy.permit: None. No wilderness permit, no quota, no lottery, and no parking pass is required at the Merritt Lake trailhead, which is unusual for this stretch of highway and worth not assuming in reverse at the other trailheads. No campfires above 5,000 feet. Use the existing sites and do not pitch on the vegetation, which is thin and slow to recover at a camp this heavily used.
bivy.notes: The eastern gateway camp. Its own trail climbs about two thousand feet in two and a half miles from around three thousand feet at the road, which is steep but short by the standards of this ridge, and it is by a wide margin the easiest way to get a loaded pack onto the crest. From here it is three and a half miles west along the ridge trail to Crescent Lake for Howard and Mastiff, and roughly three miles east to Alpine Lookout. That makes it the practical base for the eastern half of the crest and the fallback for anyone who has misjudged the traverse. Lost Lake lies just off the trail nearby and offers quieter lakeside camping if the main camp is full. Mosquitoes here in June are genuinely severe and are the most common complaint about the place. Note that the easternmost nine miles of the ridge trail, from the Lake Wenatchee end out to Alpine Lookout, are open to motorised travel, so the eastern approach is not the quiet walk the western half is.

bivy.name: Alpine Lookout — day use only, no overnight
bivy.capacity: None for the public. This is an active Forest Service fire lookout, staffed through the summer fire season, and it is NOT available to sleep in, not rentable, and not one of the lookouts in this state that take overnight visitors. Treat it as a staffed workplace: the summit is a fine place to stand, and the building is somebody's post. There is no established campsite at the lookout either, and the ground around it is narrow open ridge crest.
bivy.water: None at all, and none for the last several miles of trail in either direction. There is one seasonal spring close to the Round Mountain trailhead that runs early in the year and cannot be relied on; past it the trail is dry the whole way. From the west, the last water is Merritt Lake, about three miles back. Carry everything.
bivy.permit: A Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent annual pass is required at the Round Mountain trailhead. No wilderness permit, no quota, no lottery — none of Nason Ridge is designated wilderness. Campfires are prohibited at this elevation, and the surrounding forest is dry enough that fire restrictions are near-permanent through the summer, which is rather the point of the building on the summit.
bivy.notes: The objective itself, recorded here because the obvious question about a standing lookout has a clear answer and getting it wrong in either direction matters: you may walk to it and, if it is staffed and the lookout is willing, speak to whoever is on duty, but you may not stay in it or expect shelter from it. Plan the day accordingly and do not treat the building as a bail-out option in bad weather. The approach follows the Round Mountain trail for about a mile and a half to the ridge crest trail, then runs along the ridge with repeated ups and downs for another five miles to the lookout, roughly ten miles round trip with about 2,600 feet of gain — two thirds of that gain in the first two miles and the rest scattered along the crest. The approach can also be made from the Merritt Lake end, which is the only version of this trip that passes water. Mountain goats are frequently around the lookout and are habituated enough to approach people; keep well clear of them, never feed them, and be careful about salt on packs and clothing. Anyone needing to sleep before or after should plan on Merritt Lake to the west or the drive-in campgrounds down at the highway.

bivy.name: Mount Howard summit-area bivouac
bivy.capacity: One or two people on scraped benches just below the summit. There is no flat ground for a tent, no shelter of any kind, and nothing you would call a site — this is bare ridge crest and you are making a ledge, not finding one.
bivy.water: None, and no prospect of any. Every drop comes up from Crescent Lake, roughly two thousand feet below, and a party planning to cook and sleep here has historically carried something like four quarts each. Late-lying snow patches on the north side can be melted in early season and are gone by midsummer.
bivy.permit: None — non-wilderness, no permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass at the Rock Mountain trailhead; none required at Merritt Lake. No campfires, and there is nothing up here to burn. Leave no constructed platform behind; the crest vegetation and thin soil do not recover.
bivy.notes: Strictly a contingency and a preference, not a plan. Mount Howard is a day objective from a camp at Crescent Lake and there is no practical reason to haul water and a bag two thousand feet higher except to be on the crest at sunset and dawn, or to be positioned for a full ridge traverse taking in Mastiff to the east and Rock Mountain to the west in one push. Roughly sixty percent of sites are reservable in advance and the remainder are first come, first served. The state park campgrounds around the lake add substantially more capacity, and there are further national forest campgrounds spread along the highway corridor.
bivy.water: Piped potable water at the developed campgrounds through the operating season, and Nason Creek itself alongside. This is the one place in the file where water is a non-issue, which is why every party working this ridge should fill everything here before driving up to a trailhead rather than counting on anything above.
bivy.permit: A per-night fee, currently around the high twenties at the forest campground, with advance reservations opening well ahead and closing a few days before arrival. The state park campgrounds have their own reservation system and their own fee. No wilderness permit is involved anywhere in this zone. Fire restrictions apply in the campgrounds through the summer and are commonly total bans in late season.
bivy.notes: The drive-in base for the whole ridge, and the honest recommendation for most parties climbing these peaks: all four summits are day objectives from the highway trailheads, and sleeping at a developed campground with water and driving fifteen or twenty minutes to a trailhead beats carrying an overnight load up two thousand feet of dry switchbacks. The season runs roughly May through mid-October. From here the Merritt Lake and Round Mountain trailheads are a short drive west and north along the highway and its spurs, with Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek further west toward the pass. It is also the sensible place to reorganise mid-trip: a party that has come off the crest at one end and needs to reposition to the other has this corridor to do it in. Note that the trailheads themselves have very limited parking — Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek in particular hold only a few cars — so an early start from a nearby campground is worth more here than the extra sleep of staying further out.
