The approach follows the Round Mountain trail for about a mile and a half to the ridge crest trail, then runs along the ridge with repeated ups and downs for another five miles to the lookout, roughly ten miles round trip with about 2,600 feet of gain — two thirds of that gain in the first two miles and the rest scattered along the crest. The approach can also be made from the Merritt Lake end, which is the only version of this trip that passes water. Mountain goats are frequently around the lookout and are habituated enough to approach people; keep well clear of them, never feed them, and be careful about salt on packs and clothing. Anyone needing to sleep before or after should plan on Merritt Lake to the west or the drive-in campgrounds down at the highway.

bivy.name: Mount Howard summit-area bivouac
bivy.capacity: One or two people on scraped benches just below the summit. There is no flat ground for a tent, no shelter of any kind, and nothing you would call a site — this is bare ridge crest and you are making a ledge, not finding one.
bivy.water: None, and no prospect of any. Every drop comes up from Crescent Lake, roughly two thousand feet below, and a party planning to cook and sleep here has historically carried something like four quarts each. Late-lying snow patches on the north side can be melted in early season and are gone by midsummer.
bivy.permit: None — non-wilderness, no permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass at the Rock Mountain trailhead; none required at Merritt Lake. No campfires, and there is nothing up here to burn. Leave no constructed platform behind; the crest vegetation and thin soil do not recover.
bivy.notes: Strictly a contingency and a preference, not a plan. Mount Howard is a day objective from a camp at Crescent Lake and there is no practical reason to haul water and a bag two thousand feet higher except to be on the crest at sunset and dawn, or to be positioned for a full ridge traverse taking in Mastiff to the east and Rock Mountain to the west in one push. It has been done and it works, but it commits you: there is no water, no shelter, no escape from wind, and the descent to the nearest water is a real drop. The route up from Crescent Lake goes around the lake's northeast side and directly up the slope, threading trees and slide alder to a rock band that is turned by easy scrambling gullies onto a broad bench, and the summit is straight up the south flank from there. In spring the upper slopes hold soft snow over a firm base and are booted rather than climbed, with crampons useful on the way down; that is the season a summit camp is most often chosen, and it is also when the exposure up here bites hardest.

bivy.name: Nason Creek Campground and the Lake Wenatchee drive-in camps
bivy.capacity: Nason Creek is the closest and largest, laid out over four loops on both sides of the highway near the southeastern end of Lake Wenatchee, taking vehicles up to about thirty-five feet. Roughly sixty percent of sites are reservable in advance and the remainder are first come, first served. The state park campgrounds around the lake add substantially more capacity, and there are further national forest campgrounds spread along the highway corridor.
bivy.water: Piped potable water at the developed campgrounds through the operating season, and Nason Creek itself alongside. This is the one place in the file where water is a non-issue, which is why every party working this ridge should fill everything here before driving up to a trailhead rather than counting on anything above.
bivy.permit: A per-night fee, currently around the high twenties at the forest campground, with advance reservations opening well ahead and closing a few days before arrival. The state park campgrounds have their own reservation system and their own fee. No wilderness permit is involved anywhere in this zone. Fire restrictions apply in the campgrounds through the summer and are commonly total bans in late season.
bivy.notes: The drive-in base for the whole ridge, and the honest recommendation for most parties climbing these peaks: all four summits are day objectives from the highway trailheads, and sleeping at a developed campground with water and driving fifteen or twenty minutes to a trailhead beats carrying an overnight load up two thousand feet of dry switchbacks. The season runs roughly May through mid-October. From here the Merritt Lake and Round Mountain trailheads are a short drive west and north along the highway and its spurs, with Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek further west toward the pass. It is also the sensible place to reorganise mid-trip: a party that has come off the crest at one end and needs to reposition to the other has this corridor to do it in. Note that the trailheads themselves have very limited parking — Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek in particular hold only a few cars — so an early start from a nearby campground is worth more here than the extra sleep of staying further out.

bivy.name: Harts Pass and Meadows campgrounds
bivy.capacity: Two small Forest Service campgrounds a mile apart, five or six sites at the pass itself and roughly twice that at Meadows, first come first served with no reservations. They fill on summer weekends and in larch season, and there is no overflow up here.
bivy.water: None. Neither campground has potable water and there is no piped supply anywhere on the pass, so haul everything up from the valley or plan on filtering from creeks well below. This is the single most common mistake parties make staging here.

Forest Road 5400 climbs roughly twenty miles of unpaved single lane from Mazama with pullouts rather than passing room, a rock wall on one side and an unguarded drop on the other, and grades approaching seventeen percent on the upper ramps. Trailers are prohibited outright and motorhomes and wide vehicles are strongly discouraged. bivy.name: Windy Pass and the crest camps north of Harts Pass

bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Harts Pass, no quota and nothing to reserve. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Party size limits and any seasonal campfire ban are posted at the trailhead and change year to year, so read the board rather than assuming. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of any lake shoreline, and stock parties must carry certified weed-free feed and may not tie animals to trees overnight.

bivy.name: Hopkins Lake and Castle Pass

bivy.name: Robinson Creek valley campsites
bivy.capacity: Nine established sites are spread along the trail at roughly one and a half, two and a half, four, six, six and a half, seven and a half and nine miles from the trailhead, so a party can pick its distance rather than racing to one spot. Most take one or two tents. Stock parties use this valley heavily.
bivy.water: Good, and unusually so for this wilderness — the creek runs beside the trail for most of its length and most of the established sites hold water into the autumn. This is the one approach in the zone where water is not the limiting factor.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead kiosk, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Certified weed-free feed is required for stock and animals may not be tied directly to trees overnight or highlined within eight feet of them. Campfires are allowed in existing rings outside a burn ban, though the lower valley is dry and bans are common by late summer.
bivy.notes: The trailhead sits at about 2,560 feet just off the Harts Pass road, which means this is the low road into country whose summits stand near 8,500 — the elevation gain is the whole story. Larches turn in the last week of September and the first of October, which is also when the nights get genuinely cold at this elevation.

bivy.name: Shellrock Pass, Shellrock Basin and the Eureka Creek meadows
bivy.capacity: Dispersed rather than designated. There is a forested site by the creek at about 5,800 feet where the old Eureka Creek trail joins, a broad spread of good ground in the Eureka Creek meadows near 6,300 feet, and open camping around the pond in Shellrock Basin. Several parties can spread out through this country without seeing each other.
bivy.water: Reliable at the creek camp and in the Eureka meadows, and the pond in Shellrock Basin usually holds. The passes themselves are dry, so fill in the basin or the meadows before going up rather than expecting to find snowmelt on the crest late in the season.

Stock use is significant through here — weed-free feed is required and animals may not be tied to trees overnight. Fires are legal outside a ban but the meadows are fragile and most parties cook on a stove and leave it at that.

The standard line leaves Slate Pass, follows the Middle Fork Pasayten to Berk Creek, climbs to Freds Pass and crosses the head of Eureka Creek to Shellrock Pass, which puts a party in position to scramble Ptarmigan the following day; Dot is taken from the same country on the way through, usually in combination with the Lago and Carru group. This is genuinely remote — thirty-five miles and thirteen thousand feet of gain over four days is a fair description of a trip that collects three or four summits here — and there is no short version. The meadow ground is soft and holds a footprint for years, so pitch on the timber edge or on gravel rather than in the open grass. Snow lingers on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the single biggest constraint on when this is worth attempting.

bivy.name: Lake of the Woods and the Eureka Falls camp

Between them, though, is the crux: the creek crossing about four miles in is the last certain water before an eight-mile climb gaining five thousand feet to the pass, and in a hot late-summer spell that carry is what makes or breaks the day. Fill completely at the creek.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Monument Creek trailhead kiosk, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of the lake shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock, and the usual prohibition on tying animals to trees overnight.
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Monument Peak and Lake Mountain and it is worth being clear that they are approached from a completely different point on the Harts Pass road than the crest peaks — the Monument Creek trailhead at about 2,400 feet, roughly seven miles up from Mazama, thirteen miles short of the pass. The route runs up the Lost River valley, crosses Eureka Creek where the bridge has been out in the past, then climbs the abandoned Pistol Ridge trail to Pistol Pass at 7,100 feet before dropping to the lake. Expect around thirty miles and thirteen thousand feet over three to four days for both summits — Monument at 8,592 feet by its south ridge, Lake Mountain at 8,371 by its east ridge, each a short steep scramble from the basin. The Pistol Ridge trail is unmaintained and route-finding through it is part of the work. An alternative for parties coming from the north is to drop off Lake Mountain into Eureka Creek and camp near the south fork, which shortens things considerably if the traverse is already underway. Late September brings the larches and cold clear nights; earlier in the summer the long dry climb to the pass is punishing.

bivy.name: Copper Glance Lake
bivy.capacity: One good area at the lake taking three or four tents. That is the whole of it, so a busy autumn weekend can fill it and there is no obvious second choice nearby.
bivy.water: The lake, and it is reliable. This is the only certain water high on the approach, since the trail above the old mine works is dry through the meadows.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at the Copper Glance trailhead. Camp back from the shoreline rather than on it. The lower trail passes old mine workings on patented ground — leave the structures and hardware alone.
bivy.notes: This is the only camp that serves Big Craggy and West Craggy, and it belongs to a different drive from everything else in this zone: north from Winthrop on the West Chewuch road, then left onto the Eightmile Creek road and about twelve to thirteen miles to the trailhead at 3,800 feet. Nothing here connects to Harts Pass on foot. The trail climbs steeply for roughly two and a half miles on an old gated mining road past a washed-out bridge and the mine, then becomes a real trail through meadows on the shoulder of Big Craggy to the lake at 6,100 feet. A strong party can car-camp low on the Eightmile Creek road at one of the small Forest Service campgrounds along the creek and take both summits in one long day of about twelve miles and five thousand eight hundred feet, leaving the trail near 5,900 feet for Big Craggy's southeast ridge, then descending to the 7,600 foot saddle and picking a gully onto West Craggy's east ridge. Camping at the lake instead breaks that into something far more pleasant. The upper scree is loose and tiring on the ascent. This is an east-side approach and melts out earlier than the crest, but snow still holds above 5,500 feet well into the early summer, and the Eightmile Creek country has burned repeatedly in recent years so shade and blowdown are both unpredictable.

This is genuinely remote — thirty-five miles and thirteen thousand feet of gain over four days is a fair description of a trip that collects three or four summits here — and there is no short version. The meadow ground is soft and holds a footprint for years, so pitch on the timber edge or on gravel rather than in the open grass. Snow lingers on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the single biggest constraint on when this is worth attempting.

bivy.name: Lake of the Woods and the Eureka Falls camp
bivy.capacity: Lake of the Woods is a small alpine basin with room for a couple of tents on the benches below Lake Mountain. The Eureka Falls site down in the valley near the confluence of the Lost River and Eureka Creek is a forested camp taking a party or two. Neither is developed.
bivy.water: The lake is dependable and so is Eureka Creek down in the valley. Between them, though, is the crux: the creek crossing about four miles in is the last certain water before an eight-mile climb gaining five thousand feet to the pass, and in a hot late-summer spell that carry is what makes or breaks the day. Fill completely at the creek.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Monument Creek trailhead kiosk, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of the lake shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock, and the usual prohibition on tying animals to trees overnight.
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Monument Peak and Lake Mountain and it is worth being clear that they are approached from a completely different point on the Harts Pass road than the crest peaks — the Monument Creek trailhead at about 2,400 feet, roughly seven miles up from Mazama, thirteen miles short of the pass. The route runs up the Lost River valley, crosses Eureka Creek where the bridge has been out in the past, then climbs the abandoned Pistol Ridge trail to Pistol Pass at 7,100 feet before dropping to the lake. Expect around thirty miles and thirteen thousand feet over three to four days for both summits — Monument at 8,592 feet by its south ridge, Lake Mountain at 8,371 by its east ridge, each a short steep scramble from the basin. The Pistol Ridge trail is unmaintained and route-finding through it is part of the work. An alternative for parties coming from the north is to drop off Lake Mountain into Eureka Creek and camp near the south fork, which shortens things considerably if the traverse is already underway. Late September brings the larches and cold clear nights; earlier in the summer the long dry climb to the pass is punishing.

bivy.name: Copper Glance Lake
bivy.capacity: One good area at the lake taking three or four tents. That is the whole of it, so a busy autumn weekend can fill it and there is no obvious second choice nearby.
bivy.water: The lake, and it is reliable. This is the only certain water high on the approach, since the trail above the old mine works is dry through the meadows.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at the Copper Glance trailhead. Camp back from the shoreline rather than on it. The lower trail passes old mine workings on patented ground — leave the structures and hardware alone.
bivy.notes: This is the only camp that serves Big Craggy and West Craggy, and it belongs to a different drive from everything else in this zone: north from Winthrop on the West Chewuch road, then left onto the Eightmile Creek road and about twelve to thirteen miles to the trailhead at 3,800 feet. Nothing here connects to Harts Pass on foot. The trail climbs steeply for roughly two and a half miles on an old gated mining road past a washed-out bridge and the mine, then becomes a real trail through meadows on the shoulder of Big Craggy to the lake at 6,100 feet. A strong party can car-camp low on the Eightmile Creek road at one of the small Forest Service campgrounds along the creek and take both summits in one long day of about twelve miles and five thousand eight hundred feet, leaving the trail near 5,900 feet for Big Craggy's southeast ridge, then descending to the 7,600 foot saddle and picking a gully onto West Craggy's east ridge. Camping at the lake instead breaks that into something far more pleasant. The upper scree is loose and tiring on the ascent. This is an east-side approach and melts out earlier than the crest, but snow still holds above 5,500 feet well into the early summer, and the Eightmile Creek country has burned repeatedly in recent years so shade and blowdown are both unpredictable.

bivy.name: Harts Pass and Meadows campgrounds
bivy.capacity: Two small Forest Service campgrounds a mile apart, five or six sites at the pass itself and roughly twice that at Meadows, first come first served with no reservations. They fill on summer weekends and in larch season, and there is no overflow up here.
bivy.water: None. Neither campground has potable water and there is no piped supply anywhere on the pass, so haul everything up from the valley or plan on filtering from creeks well below. This is the single most common mistake parties make staging here.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or an Interagency pass to park at the trailheads; the campgrounds themselves are free but carry no services and no trash collection, so everything you bring comes back out. The free self-issue Pasayten wilderness permit is filled out at the trailhead kiosk before you walk in, not here. Campfires are legal in the existing rings when no burn ban is in effect, but the ground is thin alpine meadow and firewood is scarce, so most parties do without.
bivy.notes: This is the staging ground for almost everything in the zone and the road to it is a substantial fact in its own right. Forest Road 5400 climbs roughly twenty miles of unpaved single lane from Mazama with pullouts rather than passing room, a rock wall on one side and an unguarded drop on the other, and grades approaching seventeen percent on the upper ramps. Trailers are prohibited outright and motorhomes and wide vehicles are strongly discouraged. The road opens with the snowmelt, typically early to mid July and occasionally not until later, and closes with the first serious autumn storms. Above the pass it continues to the gate below Slate Peak at about 7,440 feet, the highest driveable point in the state, which puts you at a trailhead where the walking starts near 7,000 feet instead of 2,500. Four trails leave from here — the Pacific Crest Trail, the West Fork Pasayten, the Middle Fork Pasayten and Buckskin Ridge — so this one pass is the door to Osceola, Blackcap, Dot, Ptarmigan, Castle and Blizzard. Nights are cold and wind at the pass is relentless; pitch behind timber rather than in the open meadow. Note that a large lightning fire that began in mid July 2026 closed the road above the Monument Creek trailhead along with much of the northern wilderness, so confirm the road is actually open before committing to a long drive.

bivy.name: Windy Pass and the crest camps north of Harts Pass
bivy.capacity: A string of small established sites in the meadows and basins along the crest, most taking one or two tents. The Pacific Crest Trail hiking season overlaps the climbing season, so expect company at the obvious ones and be ready to walk on to the next.
bivy.water: Sparse and the defining planning problem of this stretch. There is nothing at the pass itself; the nearest campsites with water sit most of a mile further on and a couple of hundred feet higher. Carry enough for at least six miles at a time, and treat the basin between Foggy Pass and Windy Pass, the Shaw Creek crossing and the spring near Holman Peak as the fixed points to plan around rather than assuming you will find something in between.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Harts Pass, no quota and nothing to reserve. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Party size limits and any seasonal campfire ban are posted at the trailhead and change year to year, so read the board rather than assuming. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of any lake shoreline, and stock parties must carry certified weed-free feed and may not tie animals to trees overnight.
bivy.notes: This is the first day of every trip toward Castle and Blizzard and the natural stop for anyone who wants a night high on the crest without a valley grind. The trail leaves Harts Pass at about 6,200 feet, tops out just under 7,000 a little over two miles north, and never drops below 5,000 the whole way to the border, so this is sustained high open country with long views and no shelter. Snow lingers on the north-facing traverses well into the summer and those crossings are the reason most parties wait until mid August in a heavy year. Wind is the standing complaint at Windy Pass and it earns the name; camping a little below the crest costs nothing and buys a great deal. There is no mobile service anywhere along here. As pure staging these camps do nothing for the Robinson Creek or Middle Fork peaks, which go the other direction from the pass.

bivy.name: Hopkins Lake and Castle Pass
bivy.capacity: Hopkins Lake holds several small established sites in the trees around the shore and is the most comfortable camp in the far north of the wilderness. Castle Pass itself has room for a couple of parties in the timber. Neither is large and both see through-hiker traffic.
bivy.water: Hopkins Lake is the reliable one and is worth the descent for that reason alone — it is the best water for many miles in either direction. Castle Pass is drier and the sources near it are seasonal, so fill at the lake before continuing north.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Harts Pass. The international boundary matters here in a way it does not elsewhere in the zone: crossing north into Canada from the backcountry is not lawful and the long-standing arrangement that let northbound trail hikers walk out to the highway in British Columbia was ended in 2025, so there is no exit that way and no legal entry southbound either. Everything in this corner is now an out-and-back from Harts Pass. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of the lake shoreline; pull back into the trees.
bivy.notes: These are the camps that make Castle Peak and Blizzard Peak possible at all from the American side. Hopkins Lake sits about twenty-four trail miles north of Harts Pass, six hundred feet below the trail, and Castle Pass is roughly twenty-seven miles out at about 5,450 feet. Castle Peak rises directly north and east of the pass and is a scramble from a camp here; Blizzard Peak lies further east toward Frosty Pass and the Chuchuwanteen country and is more often reached by dropping down the West Fork Pasayten from Harts Pass instead, which is a different but comparably long line. Either way this is a three to five day trip for a fit party and there is no shortcut — the loss of the Canadian exit removed the only short approach that ever existed for these two summits. Plan food and water for the full round trip, expect snow on the north slopes into August, and understand that a weather change up here leaves you a very long way from the car.

bivy.name: Robinson Creek valley campsites
bivy.capacity: Nine established sites are spread along the trail at roughly one and a half, two and a half, four, six, six and a half, seven and a half and nine miles from the trailhead, so a party can pick its distance rather than racing to one spot. Most take one or two tents. Stock parties use this valley heavily.
bivy.water: Good, and unusually so for this wilderness — the creek runs beside the trail for most of its length and most of the established sites hold water into the autumn. This is the one approach in the zone where water is not the limiting factor.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead kiosk, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Certified weed-free feed is required for stock and animals may not be tied directly to trees overnight or highlined within eight feet of them. Campfires are allowed in existing rings outside a burn ban, though the lower valley is dry and bans are common by late summer.
bivy.notes: The trailhead sits at about 2,560 feet just off the Harts Pass road, which means this is the low road into country whose summits stand near 8,500 — the elevation gain is the whole story. Robinson Mountain is climbed from here by walking a little over two miles to the Beauty Creek bridge and picking up an unmaintained path just beyond it, then leaving that for open slopes above; it is fourteen miles round trip with over six thousand feet of gain and only very fit parties do it in a day, so a first night at one of the lower established sites is the sensible plan. Carrying on up the valley reaches Robinson Pass at 6,220 feet in about nine and a half miles and drops into the Middle Fork Pasayten, which is the back door to Blackcap and Osceola for anyone who would rather not start from Slate Pass. The lower valley burns and reburns, so expect open hot walking, standing dead timber and variable blowdown, and note that this drainage was inside the 2026 fire closure. Ask the district about trail conditions before building a schedule around it.

bivy.name: Doris Lake and Freds Lake basins
bivy.capacity: Informal sites on benches and ridge shoulders back from the water, room for two or three small parties without crowding. Nothing developed, no tables, no toilets.
bivy.water: Both lakes hold through the season and are the dependable supply for this whole group of peaks. Between them and the Middle Fork river flats a party can plan a multi-day traverse without rationing, which is not true of most of this wilderness.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Slate Pass or Harts Pass, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Camp at least a hundred feet back from either shoreline — the ground close to the water is thin and already worn. Weed-free feed for stock, and no tying animals to trees overnight.
bivy.notes: This is the working climbers' camp for Osceola Peak and Blackcap Mountain and the first night of the long traverse that links them with Carru and Lago. The line in starts high, which is the point: from Slate Pass at about 6,900 feet a short connector drops to the Middle Fork Pasayten trail, five miles of valley walking leads to the Ferguson Lake spur, and three more miles of climbing reaches Doris Lake at just under 7,000 feet. Osceola is then a short cross-country scramble northeast through open forest from camp, which is as close as anything in the Pasayten comes to convenient. Blackcap is further along the ridge system and is usually taken on the second or third day. Freds Lake sits on the parallel line toward Rolo Pass and serves the same purpose for parties heading for Shellrock. Reckon on three to four days for anything based here and remember that the return from a high camp means regaining Slate Pass at the end. Larches turn in the last week of September and the first of October, which is also when the nights get genuinely cold at this elevation.

bivy.name: Shellrock Pass, Shellrock Basin and the Eureka Creek meadows
bivy.capacity: Dispersed rather than designated. There is a forested site by the creek at about 5,800 feet where the old Eureka Creek trail joins, a broad spread of good ground in the Eureka Creek meadows near 6,300 feet, and open camping around the pond in Shellrock Basin. Several parties can spread out through this country without seeing each other.
bivy.water: Reliable at the creek camp and in the Eureka meadows, and the pond in Shellrock Basin usually holds. The passes themselves are dry, so fill in the basin or the meadows before going up rather than expecting to find snowmelt on the crest late in the season.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Slate Pass or Robinson Creek. Stock use is significant through here — weed-free feed is required and animals may not be tied to trees overnight. Fires are legal outside a ban but the meadows are fragile and most parties cook on a stove and leave it at that.
bivy.notes: Shellrock is the camp for Ptarmigan Peak and Dot Mountain, both of which are otherwise out of reach. The standard line leaves Slate Pass, follows the Middle Fork Pasayten to Berk Creek, climbs to Freds Pass and crosses the head of Eureka Creek to Shellrock Pass, which puts a party in position to scramble Ptarmigan the following day; Dot is taken from the same country on the way through, usually in combination with the Lago and Carru group. This is genuinely remote — thirty-five miles and thirteen thousand feet of gain over four days is a fair description of a trip that collects three or four summits here — and there is no short version. The meadow ground is soft and holds a footprint for years, so pitch on the timber edge or on gravel rather than in the open grass. Snow lingers on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the single biggest constraint on when this is worth attempting.

bivy.name: Lake of the Woods and the Eureka Falls camp
bivy.capacity: Lake of the Woods is a small alpine basin with room for a couple of tents on the benches below Lake Mountain. The Eureka Falls site down in the valley near the confluence of the Lost River and Eureka Creek is a forested camp taking a party or two. Neither is developed.
bivy.water: The lake is dependable and so is Eureka Creek down in the valley. Between them, though, is the crux: the creek crossing about four miles in is the last certain water before an eight-mile climb gaining five thousand feet to the pass, and in a hot late-summer spell that carry is what makes or breaks the day. Fill completely at the creek.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Monument Creek trailhead kiosk, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of the lake shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock, and the usual prohibition on tying animals to trees overnight.
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Monument Peak and Lake Mountain and it is worth being clear that they are approached from a completely different point on the Harts Pass road than the crest peaks — the Monument Creek trailhead at about 2,400 feet, roughly seven miles up from Mazama, thirteen miles short of the pass. The route runs up the Lost River valley, crosses Eureka Creek where the bridge has been out in the past, then climbs the abandoned Pistol Ridge trail to Pistol Pass at 7,100 feet before dropping to the lake. Expect around thirty miles and thirteen thousand feet over three to four days for both summits — Monument at 8,592 feet by its south ridge, Lake Mountain at 8,371 by its east ridge, each a short steep scramble from the basin. The Pistol Ridge trail is unmaintained and route-finding through it is part of the work. An alternative for parties coming from the north is to drop off Lake Mountain into Eureka Creek and camp near the south fork, which shortens things considerably if the traverse is already underway. Late September brings the larches and cold clear nights; earlier in the summer the long dry climb to the pass is punishing.

bivy.name: Copper Glance Lake
bivy.capacity: One good area at the lake taking three or four tents. That is the whole of it, so a busy autumn weekend can fill it and there is no obvious second choice nearby.
bivy.water: The lake, and it is reliable. This is the only certain water high on the approach, since the trail above the old mine works is dry through the meadows.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at the Copper Glance trailhead. Camp back from the shoreline rather than on it. The lower trail passes old mine workings on patented ground — leave the structures and hardware alone.
bivy.notes: This is the only camp that serves Big Craggy and West Craggy, and it belongs to a different drive from everything else in this zone: north from Winthrop on the West Chewuch road, then left onto the Eightmile Creek road and about twelve to thirteen miles to the trailhead at 3,800 feet. Nothing here connects to Harts Pass on foot. The trail climbs steeply for roughly two and a half miles on an old gated mining road past a washed-out bridge and the mine, then becomes a real trail through meadows on the shoulder of Big Craggy to the lake at 6,100 feet. A strong party can car-camp low on the Eightmile Creek road at one of the small Forest Service campgrounds along the creek and take both summits in one long day of about twelve miles and five thousand eight hundred feet, leaving the trail near 5,900 feet for Big Craggy's southeast ridge, then descending to the 7,600 foot saddle and picking a gully onto West Craggy's east ridge. Camping at the lake instead breaks that into something far more pleasant. The upper scree is loose and tiring on the ascent. This is an east-side approach and melts out earlier than the crest, but snow still holds above 5,500 feet well into the early summer, and the Eightmile Creek country has burned repeatedly in recent years so shade and blowdown are both unpredictable.

bivy.name: Kool-Aid Lake
bivy.capacity: A handful of small heather and gravel platforms around a tiny tarn, comfortable for two or three parties and crowded beyond that. No facilities, no toilet, nothing built.
bivy.water: The tarn itself plus snowmelt runnels feeding it. Reliable in July and through most of August, but it is a shallow pool with a small catchment and it can drop to a warm, silty puddle by September in a light snow year. Cache Col just above has no water at all, so parties camping high on the shoulder have to carry from here or melt snow.
bivy.permit: Once you cross Cache Col you are out of North Cascades National Park and into Glacier Peak Wilderness, so no park permit covers this camp. Sign the free self-issue wilderness register instead. If you spend a night on the park side, including at Cascade Pass or on the shoulder below the Cache Glacier, that night does need an NPS wilderness permit collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Campfires have no place at this elevation; carry a stove.
bivy.notes: The first camp on the traverse coming from Cascade Pass, reached by climbing to Cache Col and dropping a short but awkward distance southwest to the tarn. It is where the permit regime changes, which is the practical reason to know it exists even if you are only passing through. Published elevations vary by a couple of hundred feet, with figures around 6,300 the most common and one outlier several hundred feet higher, so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. From here the day ahead crosses the Red Ledge and the Middle Cascade Glacier toward Old Guard Peak and Sentinel, and there are further ridge bivouacs at around 6,300 ft just past the Red Ledge if the lake is full or the hour is late. Early season this is a snow camp with easy water everywhere; late season it is bare heather and rock and the tarn is the only source.

bivy.name: Yang Yang Lakes
bivy.capacity: Several unimproved sites in the heather between the two small lakes, enough for two or three parties. No toilet and no established platforms.
bivy.water: Two lakes, which makes this the most dependable water on the northern half of the traverse. Nothing above it is reliable: the ridge camps toward Formidable and the ground up at Le Conte Pass are snowmelt-only late in the season, though the pass usually holds tarns into midsummer.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit at the trailhead register. Camp at least 100 feet back from the lakeshores. No campfires; the ground here is thin alpine heather that does not recover.
bivy.notes: The second camp for most north-to-south parties, sitting in a shallow bowl below Le Conte Mountain after the drop off the Middle Cascade Glacier. It is the natural base for Old Guard Peak, whose summit is reached from the Le Conte Glacier above by a class 2 to 3 snow couloir and short scramble on the west side, or by two to three pitches of easy to moderate fifth class on the east ridge. Sentinel Peak is the other objective from here and the two are usually taken together. The descent into and climb out of this basin is steep on both sides, so parties running late often push instead to Le Conte Pass above and accept the thinner water. Snow lingers in the bowl well into July, which is when the camping is easiest and the heather is protected.

bivy.name: White Rock Lakes
bivy.capacity: Open benches near the outlet of the larger lake and scattered spots around the basin, wind-exposed but roomy enough for several parties. Unimproved, no toilet.
bivy.water: The lakes, fed by the snowfields and the Le Conte and Dana ice above them. Normally good all season, though the outlet stream can be reduced to a trickle late in a dry summer and the smaller pools go stagnant.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Keep camps 100 feet from the water. Stoves only.
bivy.notes: The third camp and the one most parties remember, reached from Yang Yang across the Le Conte Glacier and the Le Conte-Sentinel col, then down a long traverse under Sentinel and Old Guard. It looks straight across at Dome Peak and the Dana Glacier, which is the day that follows. Sinister Peak is not climbed from here directly, but this is the last camp with easy water before the ground gets serious: the Chickamin and Dome glaciers are the way to Sinister and to the Gunsight Range, and everything from here east is snow, ice and rock with no running water. It is a windy basin and the good sites are the sheltered ones near the outlet. Snow can cover the lakes into early July, which some parties prefer because it makes the camping flat and the water trivially available.

bivy.name: Itswoot Ridge
bivy.capacity: A string of flat heather benches along the ridge rather than one site, so several parties can spread out without crowding each other. No toilet, no built platforms.
bivy.water: Small running creeks below the lower benches, fed by snowfields on the north side of the ridge, and generally dependable through the normal climbing season. The higher benches toward the col dry out first, so drop back down for water rather than assuming it is there.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek trailhead register, plus a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle. No campfires up here.
bivy.notes: This is the working base for the southern peaks and the camp most parties coming in from Downey Creek actually use. Camps are quoted anywhere between roughly 5,900 and 6,400 ft depending on which bench you take, so the number here describes the lower, wetter end of the ridge rather than a single spot. From the benches it is moderate snow of about thirty degrees, or a scree-and-heather line on the left in late season, up to Spire Col at 7,760 ft, and from the col a short descending traverse onto the upper Dana Glacier puts you under the southeast and southwest faces of Spire Point. Dome Peak is the other objective, reached over the Dana Glacier and the Dome Glacier above. Reaching this ridge from the car is a full day with a heavy pack, so plan on arriving late and going nowhere else that evening.

bivy.name: Cub Lake
bivy.capacity: A well established camp at the lake with room for a few parties, plus meadow sites nearby. It is the most used ground in the southern half of the zone and it shows.
bivy.water: The lake, reliable all season. This is the last certain water for anyone heading up onto the ridge and glaciers, and the first on the way out.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Downey Creek trailhead. Camp 100 feet back from the shore. Practically speaking no fires, and the site is heavily enough used that the surrounding wood is already gone.
bivy.notes: Roughly 12 miles and about 3,900 ft of gain from the Downey Creek trailhead, reached by a steep switchbacking descent off the Bachelor Creek meadows and a walk around the north shore. Parties report anywhere from six hours to eleven getting here, which is a fair measure of how much the brush and the pack weight vary. It is the south-end hub: from the lake the trail climbs to Itswoot Ridge for Spire Point and Dome Peak, and everything on the Chickamin side including Sinister Peak and the Gunsight summits starts from the same ground. Because it is the established camp it also takes the impact, and there is a reasonable argument for camping on the ridge above instead where the ground is less worn, at the cost of carrying water. Coming out, this is where the traverse ends and the brush begins.

bivy.name: Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
bivy.capacity: Rough forest sites and a meadow flat near the head of the creek, party-sized only. Nothing established, no toilet.
bivy.water: Bachelor Creek runs the whole way and is never the problem. The creek crossing itself can be, in high water or early season.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at Downey Creek. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but the ground is wet forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
bivy.notes: This exists because of the brush, and the brush is the single most important thing to understand about the south end. From the Downey Creek trailhead at 1,440 ft the Downey Creek trail runs about six easy forested miles to Sixmile Camp; after that the abandoned Bachelor Creek trail deteriorates badly. The first two miles are tolerable, then it crosses to the south side and turns into slide alder and avalanche deadfall, with reports of sixty or more trees over the trail and long sections where following it is closer to bushwhacking than hiking. Parties routinely take nine to eleven hours from the car to Cub Lake and a slow group with heavy packs can lose the trail entirely. Splitting the approach with a night around the 4,500 ft meadows near the head of the creek is the honest answer for anyone who is not fast, and it is why some parties choose to enter from Cascade Pass and exit here rather than the other way round, so the brush is done downhill and with lighter packs. There is a north-side line through open forest paralleling the creek that some report as better than the trail itself. Everything about this approach is currently harder than the above suggests: the Suiattle River Road is closed to vehicles at about milepost 4 after flood damage, under an order running to the start of 2028 unless lifted sooner, which leaves roughly sixteen extra road miles each way to a trailhead at mile 20. The road also spent about a decade closed before reopening in 2014, so a long closure here is the normal state of affairs rather than a surprise. Confirm the road before committing to this end.

bivy.name: Spire Col bivouac
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on the col itself, with further spots scattered along the ridge below it. Rock and snow, nothing flat and nothing built.
bivy.water: None. Melt snow, or carry from the creeks below Itswoot Ridge. In late season the snow near the col can be gone entirely and then there is nothing at all.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than on the heather. Pack out human waste; there is no toilet anywhere on this side of the zone.
bivy.notes: The col at 7,760 ft between Itswoot Ridge and the upper Dana Glacier, and the highest useful bivouac for Spire Point. Taking it saves an hour or more off summit morning on the Southwest Face and puts you above the section of snow that softens in the afternoon. It is fully exposed, cold, and windy, which is the trade. Parties heading on to Dome Peak sometimes use it too, though the Dome Glacier camps further east are better placed for that. Treat this as a fair-weather option: there is no shelter, and retreating from here in bad weather means downclimbing snow you came up in daylight.

bivy.name: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
bivy.capacity: Rock rings and cleared platforms for one or two parties at a time. At the Dome-Chickamin col there is a flat, large, windy option on the west side and a smaller, harder, calmer one on the east. Nothing else, and no toilet.
bivy.water: None running. Every drop is melted snow, and on bare ice years even that takes hunting for. Carry what you can from Cub Lake or the Itswoot Ridge creeks and plan the fuel for melting.

Snow lingers in the bowl well into July, which is when the camping is easiest and the heather is protected.

bivy.name: White Rock Lakes
bivy.capacity: Open benches near the outlet of the larger lake and scattered spots around the basin, wind-exposed but roomy enough for several parties. Unimproved, no toilet.
bivy.water: The lakes, fed by the snowfields and the Le Conte and Dana ice above them. Normally good all season, though the outlet stream can be reduced to a trickle late in a dry summer and the smaller pools go stagnant.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Keep camps 100 feet from the water. Stoves only.
bivy.notes: The third camp and the one most parties remember, reached from Yang Yang across the Le Conte Glacier and the Le Conte-Sentinel col, then down a long traverse under Sentinel and Old Guard. bivy.name: Itswoot Ridge
bivy.capacity: A string of flat heather benches along the ridge rather than one site, so several parties can spread out without crowding each other. No toilet, no built platforms.

bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek trailhead register, plus a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle. No campfires up here.

bivy.name: Cub Lake
bivy.capacity: A well established camp at the lake with room for a few parties, plus meadow sites nearby. It is the most used ground in the southern half of the zone and it shows.
bivy.water: The lake, reliable all season. This is the last certain water for anyone heading up onto the ridge and glaciers, and the first on the way out.

Coming out, this is where the traverse ends and the brush begins.

bivy.name: Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
bivy.capacity: Rough forest sites and a meadow flat near the head of the creek, party-sized only. Nothing established, no toilet.
bivy.water: Bachelor Creek runs the whole way and is never the problem. The creek crossing itself can be, in high water or early season.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at Downey Creek. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but the ground is wet forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
bivy.notes: This exists because of the brush, and the brush is the single most important thing to understand about the south end. From the Downey Creek trailhead at 1,440 ft the Downey Creek trail runs about six easy forested miles to Sixmile Camp; after that the abandoned Bachelor Creek trail deteriorates badly. The first two miles are tolerable, then it crosses to the south side and turns into slide alder and avalanche deadfall, with reports of sixty or more trees over the trail and long sections where following it is closer to bushwhacking than hiking. Parties routinely take nine to eleven hours from the car to Cub Lake and a slow group with heavy packs can lose the trail entirely. Splitting the approach with a night around the 4,500 ft meadows near the head of the creek is the honest answer for anyone who is not fast, and it is why some parties choose to enter from Cascade Pass and exit here rather than the other way round, so the brush is done downhill and with lighter packs. There is a north-side line through open forest paralleling the creek that some report as better than the trail itself. Everything about this approach is currently harder than the above suggests: the Suiattle River Road is closed to vehicles at about milepost 4 after flood damage, under an order running to the start of 2028 unless lifted sooner, which leaves roughly sixteen extra road miles each way to a trailhead at mile 20. The road also spent about a decade closed before reopening in 2014, so a long closure here is the normal state of affairs rather than a surprise. Confirm the road before committing to this end.

bivy.name: Spire Col bivouac
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on the col itself, with further spots scattered along the ridge below it. Rock and snow, nothing flat and nothing built.
bivy.water: None. Melt snow, or carry from the creeks below Itswoot Ridge. In late season the snow near the col can be gone entirely and then there is nothing at all.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than on the heather. Pack out human waste; there is no toilet anywhere on this side of the zone.
bivy.notes: The col at 7,760 ft between Itswoot Ridge and the upper Dana Glacier, and the highest useful bivouac for Spire Point. Taking it saves an hour or more off summit morning on the Southwest Face and puts you above the section of snow that softens in the afternoon. It is fully exposed, cold, and windy, which is the trade. Parties heading on to Dome Peak sometimes use it too, though the Dome Glacier camps further east are better placed for that. Treat this as a fair-weather option: there is no shelter, and retreating from here in bad weather means downclimbing snow you came up in daylight.

bivy.name: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
bivy.capacity: Rock rings and cleared platforms for one or two parties at a time. At the Dome-Chickamin col there is a flat, large, windy option on the west side and a smaller, harder, calmer one on the east. Nothing else, and no toilet.
bivy.water: None running. Every drop is melted snow, and on bare ice years even that takes hunting for. Carry what you can from Cub Lake or the Itswoot Ridge creeks and plan the fuel for melting.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek register. Camp on snow, rock or ice. Pack out human waste, which matters more here than anywhere else in the zone because the meltwater below runs straight into the glacier-fed creeks.

bivy.name: Kool-Aid Lake
bivy.capacity: A handful of small heather and gravel platforms around a tiny tarn, comfortable for two or three parties and crowded beyond that. No facilities, no toilet, nothing built.
bivy.water: The tarn itself plus snowmelt runnels feeding it. Reliable in July and through most of August, but it is a shallow pool with a small catchment and it can drop to a warm, silty puddle by September in a light snow year. Cache Col just above has no water at all, so parties camping high on the shoulder have to carry from here or melt snow.
bivy.permit: Once you cross Cache Col you are out of North Cascades National Park and into Glacier Peak Wilderness, so no park permit covers this camp. Sign the free self-issue wilderness register instead. If you spend a night on the park side, including at Cascade Pass or on the shoulder below the Cache Glacier, that night does need an NPS wilderness permit collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Campfires have no place at this elevation; carry a stove.
bivy.notes: The first camp on the traverse coming from Cascade Pass, reached by climbing to Cache Col and dropping a short but awkward distance southwest to the tarn. It is where the permit regime changes, which is the practical reason to know it exists even if you are only passing through. Published elevations vary by a couple of hundred feet, with figures around 6,300 the most common and one outlier several hundred feet higher, so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. From here the day ahead crosses the Red Ledge and the Middle Cascade Glacier toward Old Guard Peak and Sentinel, and there are further ridge bivouacs at around 6,300 ft just past the Red Ledge if the lake is full or the hour is late. Early season this is a snow camp with easy water everywhere; late season it is bare heather and rock and the tarn is the only source.

bivy.name: Yang Yang Lakes
bivy.capacity: Several unimproved sites in the heather between the two small lakes, enough for two or three parties. No toilet and no established platforms.
bivy.water: Two lakes, which makes this the most dependable water on the northern half of the traverse. Nothing above it is reliable: the ridge camps toward Formidable and the ground up at Le Conte Pass are snowmelt-only late in the season, though the pass usually holds tarns into midsummer.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit at the trailhead register. Camp at least 100 feet back from the lakeshores. No campfires; the ground here is thin alpine heather that does not recover.
bivy.notes: The second camp for most north-to-south parties, sitting in a shallow bowl below Le Conte Mountain after the drop off the Middle Cascade Glacier. It is the natural base for Old Guard Peak, whose summit is reached from the Le Conte Glacier above by a class 2 to 3 snow couloir and short scramble on the west side, or by two to three pitches of easy to moderate fifth class on the east ridge. bivy.name: Spire Col bivouac
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on the col itself, with further spots scattered along the ridge below it. Rock and snow, nothing flat and nothing built.

bivy.name: Scatter Lake basin
bivy.capacity: Several established tent sites around the lake, plus a stock camp in the meadow about a mile below it. Small basin, and it fills on larch weekends in late September and early October.
bivy.water: The lake itself, and Scatter Creek is beside the trail for most of the climb. This is one of the more reliable water situations in the zone.
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit is needed to hike or camp on the Forest Service side of this range. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at the Scatter Creek trailhead. Fill in the trailhead register where one is present. Firewood is scarce and the lakeshore vegetation is fragile, so treat this as a stove-only camp regardless of whether a formal fire ban is posted, and expect an actual east-side fire restriction from midsummer into September in most years.
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Abernathy Peak and it sits directly under both of its routes. From Twisp the Twisp River road runs about 22 miles, turning off on an unpaved spur immediately after the Scatter Creek crossing; pavement ends several miles before that. The trail is a hard 4.6 miles with roughly 3,800 ft of gain to a lake just under 7,000 ft, so most parties either take the whole day to reach it or accept a long day out and back. From camp the South Ridge is the straightforward line, a steep loose scree slog above the lake, and the North Ridge is reached by working around the basin. The whole face above the lake has a southern aspect and is normally snow free from early July; before that, expect firm snow in the gully and an ice axe is not optional. Late September and the first week of October is the classic window here for the larch, and it is also when the basin is busiest. Bring what you need for a cold dry camp: this is east-side country, the nights are colder than the drive up suggests, and there is no shelter of any kind.

bivy.name: Reynolds Creek upper basin
bivy.capacity: Informal sites in the upper basin, a handful of parties at most. No numbered sites, no toilet, nothing built.
bivy.water: Reynolds Creek runs through the basin and is the reason to camp here rather than higher. Filter it. Above the basin the slopes are dry talus and scree with nothing until you are back down.
bivy.permit: Forest Service ground, no overnight permit needed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the trailhead. Stove only in practice - fires are usually restricted here through the dry months and there is little to burn.
bivy.notes: The obvious camp for the Reynolds Peak scramble, and it turns an 11-mile day with 5,300 ft of gain into a comfortable two. Access is easy to get wrong: drive the Twisp River road about 19 miles to Mystery Campground, cross the river there on the forest road, and follow it a little over a mile to a junction and then to the Reynolds Creek trailhead at around 3,100 ft. Mystery Campground itself is the fallback if you arrive late and want a roadside night before starting. Follow the Reynolds Creek trail on the north side of the creek to somewhere above 4,800 ft, where a log crossing puts you into the basin. Camp there, with water and views, and the summit is then a scree and talus grind to a short easy scramble through the summit rocks. Snow lingers in the upper basin later than the sunny Sawtooth crest to the south because this side faces roughly north, so early July trips should expect snow on the approach slopes. The valley has burned in places in recent seasons and blowdown on the lower trail is a recurring nuisance; check the current trail report rather than assuming a clean tread.

bivy.name: Oval Lakes basin - West and Middle Oval
bivy.capacity: Good sites all around West Oval, with a marked pit toilet, and stock camping with grazing in the basin above Middle Oval. The largest camping capacity in the northern half of the range.
bivy.water: The lakes. Reliable all season. The long climb in from Eagle Creek has water low down and then very little, so carry enough for the ascent.
bivy.permit: No overnight permit on the Forest Service side. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at the Eagle Creek-Oval trailhead. Pack out your own toilet paper even where a pit toilet exists. Fires are a bad idea here even when legal, and are usually banned outright by August.
bivy.notes: This is the base for Oval Peak and the northern approach to Courtney and Star, all three of which are walk-and-scramble summits off the Chelan Summit trail once you are on the crest. It is not a casual trip: about 20 miles round trip with close to 6,700 ft of gain, up an old moraine below Gray Peak, onto the Chelan Summit trail, over a pass east of Gray Peak, and down into the basin where the maintained trail ends at Middle Oval. Much of that approach burned in the 2018 Crescent Mountain fire and is now open, dusty and hot with standing snags; do it early in the day, expect no shade, and be wary of dead trees in wind. From camp the Oval Peak scramble is short, and a fit party can link Courtney and Star along the crest, though it is a long day. Late July through early October is the practical season, with the larch turning in late September. The same basin can be reached from the lake side by ferry to Moore Point and up Fish Creek, which is the way in for a party that would rather ride a boat than drive the Twisp River road.

bivy.name: Libby Lake
bivy.capacity: A few small sites below the lake, and rougher ground around it. Room for two or three parties without crowding; the shoreline is fragile and there is little flat ground.
bivy.water: The lake, and Libby Creek along the trail below. The last several hundred feet of the climb are dry.
bivy.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Libby Lake trailhead. This is a high, sparse, slow-growing basin; carry a stove and do not build a fire, and expect a formal restriction across the lower Methow through the summer.
bivy.notes: The camp for both Raven Ridge routes and the usual base for Hoodoo Peak. Getting here is a different drive from the Twisp River trailheads: from Twisp go east on Highway 20 then south on Highway 153 about nine miles and turn up the Libby Creek road. The trail is a steep 5.3 miles to a lake at roughly 7,600 ft, gaining well over 3,000 ft, and it passes the remains of an old cabin at around four miles that makes a lower alternative camp if you run out of daylight or want water lower down. Raven Ridge rises about 800 ft directly above the lake, and the standard gully-and-ridge line starts from the shore, so this is as close as a camp gets to a route in this range. Hoodoo is a scramble from the same basin, and strong parties climb both in a day from here. The upper basin holds snow into July and the gullies can be firm and unpleasant early; late August through the first half of October is the good window, and the larch here is as good as anywhere in the Sawtooth. It is exposed and treeless at the lake, so a camp below the outlet is more comfortable in wind.

bivy.name: Upper Eagle Lake and Horsehead Pass
bivy.capacity: Many sites - almost every level spot around Upper Eagle Lake gets used, plus a large horse camp just below it and further sites at Lower Eagle Lake about a mile off the main trail. This is the busiest backcountry camping in the range.
bivy.water: Both Eagle Lakes, and Eagle Creek is bridged on the way up. Above the lakes, on the pass and along the crest, there is nothing; carry water for any traverse day.
bivy.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit needed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Eagle Lakes / Crater Creek trailhead. This trail is open to motorcycles and stock as well as walkers, which surprises people. Fires are restricted most summers and firewood at 7,000 ft is not a renewable resource here.
bivy.notes: The hub of the southern Sawtooth and the practical base for Switchback Mountain, with Hoodoo and Raven Ridge also within reach along the crest. Access is the Gold Creek side, not the Twisp River: turn off the highway onto the North Fork Gold Creek road, then a signed spur for several miles to the Eagle Lakes trailhead at about 4,760 ft. It is roughly 12.5 miles round trip to Upper Eagle Lake at 7,110 ft with only about 2,350 ft of gain, so it is a gentle carry by the standards of this range. Lower Eagle Lake at about 6,490 ft is the quieter option. Horsehead Pass at roughly 7,540 ft sits just above camp and is the gateway both to Boiling Lake on the far side and to the ridge walking that reaches Switchback. Linking on to Martin Lakes and Cooney Lake makes a longer circuit that takes in more of the southern summits. Season is roughly July into October; the pass holds snow on its north side later than the approach suggests. Be aware that Upper Eagle can be crowded and noisy on a fine weekend - if you want quiet, camp at Lower Eagle or push over the pass.

bivy.name: Boiling Lake basin
bivy.capacity: Established sites at the lake and near the outlet, clearly heavily used. Room for several parties. No facilities.
bivy.water: The lake and its outlet, reliable through the season. The Chelan Summit trail on either side is long and dry in places, so fill here.
bivy.permit: Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness, Forest Service, so no overnight permit. If you arrive by boat and stay on the trail system you need no permit at all; if you drive, a Northwest Forest Pass covers the parking. Expect fire restrictions from midsummer, and treat the basin as stove only in any case.
bivy.notes: The high camp for Star Peak and Courtney Peak, sitting on the west side of the crest under Sawtooth Ridge, and the natural meeting point of the two access systems. From the road it is reached over Horsehead Pass from Upper Eagle Lake in a short day. From the water it is the first high camp on the Chelan Summit trail after the long climb up from the Prince Creek boat landing, which is where most multi-day traverses of this range put their first night on the crest. Both Star and Courtney are scrambles from here and the pair is a reasonable single day. The position is the value: it is high, it is on the crest, and it is on water, which in this dry east-side range is an unusual combination. It is popular and it shows, so camp on existing ground rather than making new. Season is roughly mid-July to mid-October. There is no shelter and no trees worth the name at the lake, so plan for wind, and for a cold clear night at this elevation even in August.

bivy.name: Prince Creek Campground - boat-in
bivy.capacity: A developed lakeside camp with tables, fire grates and a toilet. Sizeable, and the standard first or last night for anyone traversing the range from the water.

bivy.name: Bird Creek Camp, Devore Creek trail

bivy.water: Bird Creek is immediately past the camp; the site sits about a hundred feet short of the crossing. Parties going higher can camp near 5,800 ft in the Bird Creek drainage, where there is water in early and mid-season but which can dry out late.

bivy.name: Scatter Lake basin
bivy.capacity: Several established tent sites around the lake, plus a stock camp in the meadow about a mile below it. Small basin, and it fills on larch weekends in late September and early October.
bivy.water: The lake itself, and Scatter Creek is beside the trail for most of the climb. This is one of the more reliable water situations in the zone.
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit is needed to hike or camp on the Forest Service side of this range. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at the Scatter Creek trailhead. Fill in the trailhead register where one is present. bivy.notes: This is the camp for Abernathy Peak and it sits directly under both of its routes. From Twisp the Twisp River road runs about 22 miles, turning off on an unpaved spur immediately after the Scatter Creek crossing; pavement ends several miles before that. The trail is a hard 4.6 miles with roughly 3,800 ft of gain to a lake just under 7,000 ft, so most parties either take the whole day to reach it or accept a long day out and back. From camp the South Ridge is the straightforward line, a steep loose scree slog above the lake, and the North Ridge is reached by working around the basin. The whole face above the lake has a southern aspect and is normally snow free from early July; before that, expect firm snow in the gully and an ice axe is not optional. bivy.name: Reynolds Creek upper basin
bivy.capacity: Informal sites in the upper basin, a handful of parties at most. No numbered sites, no toilet, nothing built.
bivy.water: Reynolds Creek runs through the basin and is the reason to camp here rather than higher. Filter it. Above the basin the slopes are dry talus and scree with nothing until you are back down.
bivy.permit: Forest Service ground, no overnight permit needed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the trailhead. Stove only in practice - fires are usually restricted here through the dry months and there is little to burn.
bivy.notes: The obvious camp for the Reynolds Peak scramble, and it turns an 11-mile day with 5,300 ft of gain into a comfortable two. Access is easy to get wrong: drive the Twisp River road about 19 miles to Mystery Campground, cross the river there on the forest road, and follow it a little over a mile to a junction and then to the Reynolds Creek trailhead at around 3,100 ft. Mystery Campground itself is the fallback if you arrive late and want a roadside night before starting. Follow the Reynolds Creek trail on the north side of the creek to somewhere above 4,800 ft, where a log crossing puts you into the basin. Camp there, with water and views, and the summit is then a scree and talus grind to a short easy scramble through the summit rocks. Snow lingers in the upper basin later than the sunny Sawtooth crest to the south because this side faces roughly north, so early July trips should expect snow on the approach slopes. The valley has burned in places in recent seasons and blowdown on the lower trail is a recurring nuisance; check the current trail report rather than assuming a clean tread.

bivy.name: Oval Lakes basin - West and Middle Oval
bivy.capacity: Good sites all around West Oval, with a marked pit toilet, and stock camping with grazing in the basin above Middle Oval. The largest camping capacity in the northern half of the range.
bivy.water: The lakes. Reliable all season. The long climb in from Eagle Creek has water low down and then very little, so carry enough for the ascent.
bivy.permit: No overnight permit on the Forest Service side. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at the Eagle Creek-Oval trailhead. Pack out your own toilet paper even where a pit toilet exists. Fires are a bad idea here even when legal, and are usually banned outright by August.
bivy.notes: This is the base for Oval Peak and the northern approach to Courtney and Star, all three of which are walk-and-scramble summits off the Chelan Summit trail once you are on the crest. Much of that approach burned in the 2018 Crescent Mountain fire and is now open, dusty and hot with standing snags; do it early in the day, expect no shade, and be wary of dead trees in wind. From camp the Oval Peak scramble is short, and a fit party can link Courtney and Star along the crest, though it is a long day. Late July through early October is the practical season, with the larch turning in late September. The same basin can be reached from the lake side by ferry to Moore Point and up Fish Creek, which is the way in for a party that would rather ride a boat than drive the Twisp River road.

bivy.name: Libby Lake
bivy.capacity: A few small sites below the lake, and rougher ground around it. Room for two or three parties without crowding; the shoreline is fragile and there is little flat ground.
bivy.water: The lake, and Libby Creek along the trail below. The last several hundred feet of the climb are dry.

Getting here is a different drive from the Twisp River trailheads: from Twisp go east on Highway 20 then south on Highway 153 about nine miles and turn up the Libby Creek road. bivy.name: Upper Eagle Lake and Horsehead Pass
bivy.capacity: Many sites - almost every level spot around Upper Eagle Lake gets used, plus a large horse camp just below it and further sites at Lower Eagle Lake about a mile off the main trail. This is the busiest backcountry camping in the range.
bivy.water: Both Eagle Lakes, and Eagle Creek is bridged on the way up. Above the lakes, on the pass and along the crest, there is nothing; carry water for any traverse day.
bivy.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit needed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Eagle Lakes / Crater Creek trailhead. This trail is open to motorcycles and stock as well as walkers, which surprises people. Fires are restricted most summers and firewood at 7,000 ft is not a renewable resource here.
bivy.notes: The hub of the southern Sawtooth and the practical base for Switchback Mountain, with Hoodoo and Raven Ridge also within reach along the crest. Access is the Gold Creek side, not the Twisp River: turn off the highway onto the North Fork Gold Creek road, then a signed spur for several miles to the Eagle Lakes trailhead at about 4,760 ft. Lower Eagle Lake at about 6,490 ft is the quieter option. Linking on to Martin Lakes and Cooney Lake makes a longer circuit that takes in more of the southern summits. Season is roughly July into October; the pass holds snow on its north side later than the approach suggests. Be aware that Upper Eagle can be crowded and noisy on a fine weekend - if you want quiet, camp at Lower Eagle or push over the pass.

Expect fire restrictions from midsummer, and treat the basin as stove only in any case.
