bivy.water: The lake, and Libby Creek along the trail below. The last several hundred feet of the climb are dry.
bivy.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Libby Lake trailhead. This is a high, sparse, slow-growing basin; carry a stove and do not build a fire, and expect a formal restriction across the lower Methow through the summer.
bivy.notes: The camp for both Raven Ridge routes and the usual base for Hoodoo Peak. Getting here is a different drive from the Twisp River trailheads: from Twisp go east on Highway 20 then south on Highway 153 about nine miles and turn up the Libby Creek road. The trail is a steep 5.3 miles to a lake at roughly 7,600 ft, gaining well over 3,000 ft, and it passes the remains of an old cabin at around four miles that makes a lower alternative camp if you run out of daylight or want water lower down. Raven Ridge rises about 800 ft directly above the lake, and the standard gully-and-ridge line starts from the shore, so this is as close as a camp gets to a route in this range. Hoodoo is a scramble from the same basin, and strong parties climb both in a day from here. The upper basin holds snow into July and the gullies can be firm and unpleasant early; late August through the first half of October is the good window, and the larch here is as good as anywhere in the Sawtooth. It is exposed and treeless at the lake, so a camp below the outlet is more comfortable in wind.

bivy.name: Upper Eagle Lake and Horsehead Pass
bivy.capacity: Many sites - almost every level spot around Upper Eagle Lake gets used, plus a large horse camp just below it and further sites at Lower Eagle Lake about a mile off the main trail. This is the busiest backcountry camping in the range.
bivy.water: Both Eagle Lakes, and Eagle Creek is bridged on the way up. Above the lakes, on the pass and along the crest, there is nothing; carry water for any traverse day.
bivy.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit needed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Eagle Lakes / Crater Creek trailhead. This trail is open to motorcycles and stock as well as walkers, which surprises people. Fires are restricted most summers and firewood at 7,000 ft is not a renewable resource here.
bivy.notes: The hub of the southern Sawtooth and the practical base for Switchback Mountain, with Hoodoo and Raven Ridge also within reach along the crest. Access is the Gold Creek side, not the Twisp River: turn off the highway onto the North Fork Gold Creek road, then a signed spur for several miles to the Eagle Lakes trailhead at about 4,760 ft. It is roughly 12.5 miles round trip to Upper Eagle Lake at 7,110 ft with only about 2,350 ft of gain, so it is a gentle carry by the standards of this range. Lower Eagle Lake at about 6,490 ft is the quieter option. Horsehead Pass at roughly 7,540 ft sits just above camp and is the gateway both to Boiling Lake on the far side and to the ridge walking that reaches Switchback. Linking on to Martin Lakes and Cooney Lake makes a longer circuit that takes in more of the southern summits. Season is roughly July into October; the pass holds snow on its north side later than the approach suggests. Be aware that Upper Eagle can be crowded and noisy on a fine weekend - if you want quiet, camp at Lower Eagle or push over the pass.

bivy.name: Boiling Lake basin
bivy.capacity: Established sites at the lake and near the outlet, clearly heavily used. Room for several parties. No facilities.
bivy.water: The lake and its outlet, reliable through the season. The Chelan Summit trail on either side is long and dry in places, so fill here.
bivy.permit: Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness, Forest Service, so no overnight permit. If you arrive by boat and stay on the trail system you need no permit at all; if you drive, a Northwest Forest Pass covers the parking. Expect fire restrictions from midsummer, and treat the basin as stove only in any case.
bivy.notes: The high camp for Star Peak and Courtney Peak, sitting on the west side of the crest under Sawtooth Ridge, and the natural meeting point of the two access systems. From the road it is reached over Horsehead Pass from Upper Eagle Lake in a short day. From the water it is the first high camp on the Chelan Summit trail after the long climb up from the Prince Creek boat landing, which is where most multi-day traverses of this range put their first night on the crest. Both Star and Courtney are scrambles from here and the pair is a reasonable single day. The position is the value: it is high, it is on the crest, and it is on water, which in this dry east-side range is an unusual combination. It is popular and it shows, so camp on existing ground rather than making new. Season is roughly mid-July to mid-October. There is no shelter and no trees worth the name at the lake, so plan for wind, and for a cold clear night at this elevation even in August.

bivy.name: Prince Creek Campground - boat-in
bivy.capacity: A developed lakeside camp with tables, fire grates and a toilet. Sizeable, and the standard first or last night for anyone traversing the range from the water.
bivy.water: Prince Creek and the lake. From here the Chelan Summit trail climbs thousands of feet with long dry stretches - this is the last easy water for a long time, so leave with full bottles.
bivy.permit: Forest Service, and no permit is needed to hike or camp along this stretch if you have been dropped by boat. The rules change further up the lake: the National Park Service boundary sits between here and Stehekin, and any camp inside the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area - Flick Creek, Weaver Point and everything nearer the head of the lake - needs a North Cascades backcountry permit, which is itinerary-based, allocated partly by an early-season lottery for the peak months and partly walk-up. Fires are permitted in the established grates here, but open fires are banned outright at several of the Park Service camps up-lake, and a valley-wide ban is common by late summer. The real constraint is the ferry: the up-lake passenger boat must be booked ahead in season, Prince Creek is a request stop rather than a scheduled one and can be skipped in poor conditions, and a missed pickup on the return means a long walk to Stehekin.
bivy.notes: The lake-side gateway to Star, Courtney and the southern crest. The boat drops you at roughly 1,100 ft, lake level, and the Chelan Summit trail climbs from there toward Boiling Lake and the Sawtooth crest - a serious first day in heat, on a south-facing slope, with almost no shade. Most parties land in the afternoon, camp here, and start the climb at first light. The other useful boat stop is Moore Point, about ten miles further up-lake and five and a half below Stehekin, a smaller camp with a dock, a picnic shelter, food storage and a toilet, from which the Fish Creek trail climbs to Round Lake and the Oval Lakes country - that is the water-side way to Oval Peak. The Lakeshore trail connecting the two took heavy damage in the storms of December 2025, with debris flows and washouts between Prince Creek and Moore Point, and Moore Point has also been closed at times for post-fire flood risk, so confirm both the camp and the trail are open before committing to an itinerary that depends on walking between them. The lake side is snow-free far earlier than the crest, often from April, which makes it the way in for an early-season trip.

bivy.name: Bird Creek Camp, Devore Creek trail
bivy.capacity: Three small tent openings and a fire ring - room for perhaps four small tents. Very small, and there is no overflow.
bivy.water: Bird Creek is immediately past the camp; the site sits about a hundred feet short of the crossing. Below here, Devore Creek is the last dependable water on the climb, so fill there if you are unsure. Parties going higher can camp near 5,800 ft in the Bird Creek drainage, where there is water in early and mid-season but which can dry out late.
bivy.permit: This is inside the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area, so a North Cascades backcountry permit is required year-round for the overnight, tied to a specific camp and itinerary. Peak-season demand is high enough that an early-access lottery governs the best dates and the odds are poor; plan around it rather than hoping. Open fires are banned at several camps in this unit and restricted to established pits elsewhere, and a total ban is normal by late summer. The ferry and the Stehekin shuttle are the other half of the planning: the boat must be booked, the shuttle up the valley runs a limited seasonal schedule, and the Company Creek road trailhead is several miles from the landing, so missing a bus costs you a half day on foot.
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Devore Peak and Tupshin Peak, and it is worth being clear that these two are not a Sawtooth trip. They stand west of Lake Chelan on the long ridge dividing Company Creek and Hilgard Creek from Devore Creek, and everything about them - the wilderness, the permit system, the transport - is different from the Twisp River peaks. The usual way in is a ferry to the Stehekin landing, then the Company Creek road, with the Devore Creek trail reached from Weaver Point on the far side of the head of the lake; Bird Creek Camp sits about four miles up that trail at around 4,200 ft. From here Tupshin's South Ridge and Devore's Southeast Ridge are both reachable, and parties commonly climb both from the same base, either from this camp or from a higher bivouac around 5,800 ft in the Bird Creek basin. Both are steep, brushy and loose by reputation and neither is a walk-up. The season is roughly late July into early October; the approach is low, hot and overgrown early, and the upper slopes hold snow. This is the least forgiving logistics in the zone - a party that misses a boat or a bus loses a day at each end - so build slack into the itinerary and carry more food than the schedule strictly needs.

bivy.name: Bean Creek Basin meadows
bivy.capacity: A stand of trees at the edge of the meadow holds four or more multi-tent sites, and there are scattered singles beyond it; two or three parties fit comfortably and it fills on summer weekends. No toilet of any kind.
bivy.water: Bean Creek runs through the basin and is the reason the camp is here, but it is a small east-side creek and by late August only one of the several channels may still be running. The dependable fill is lower down, where the trail crosses Bean Creek at the split with the Earl Peak branch — top off there rather than assuming the basin will provide, and assume nothing at all above the basin, because the climb to Earl Pass and the whole southwest ridge are dry.
bivy.permit: No permit and no quota. Nothing here is inside the Enchantment Permit Area and there is no lottery of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent annual pass is needed to park at the Beverly Creek trailhead. Where a trail from this basin crosses into the Alpine Lakes Wilderness further north, the free self-issue slip from the trailhead box covers it. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet in this national forest, which includes the basin, and the whole valley routinely falls under a total burn ban from midsummer onward. Camp on bare ground or duff, never on the meadow itself.
bivy.notes: This is the overnight base for Earl Peak, and it is a contingency rather than the plan — Earl is a straightforward day from the car for most parties, and the reason to sleep here is a late start, a slow party, or a wish to link Earl with Bean Peak and the surrounding scrambles over two days. From the Beverly Creek trailhead at about 3,600 feet, take the right-hand branch at the first junction half a mile in and climb steeply up the Bean Creek valley, crossing the creek to reach the basin at roughly two miles. From the basin the route continues to Earl Pass on the divide between Bean and Standup Creeks at about 6,200 feet, then turns north up the southwest ridge, which carries bits of boot tread most of the way and stays easy scrambling to the summit. The basin is a flower meadow in early July and dry gold by September; mosquitoes are bad from snowmelt through mid-July. The last mile and a half of road to the trailhead is a rough, overgrown one-lane track that punishes a low car.

bivy.name: Beverly Turnpike camps at the Fourth Creek junction
bivy.capacity: A cluster of good sites near the creek holding four or five tents, spread over enough ground that two parties are not on top of each other
bivy.water: Beverly Creek runs briskly right beside the camp and is the most reliable water anywhere in this group of peaks. That reliability ends abruptly at the junction: the sites up on the saddle where the Fourth Creek and Hardscrabble trails meet are dry, and there is nothing on the climb to Iron Peak's saddle from this side. A small running source sits roughly four tenths of a mile down the Hardscrabble side of that saddle, off-trail, and is worth knowing about if you have committed to the high ground and misjudged.
bivy.permit: No permit, no quota, no lottery. Northwest Forest Pass at the Beverly Creek trailhead. The free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness slip from the trailhead box covers travel where the trails cross the boundary north of here. No campfires above 5,000 feet, and expect a valley-wide burn ban from midsummer; this is dry, brittle east-side timber that has already carried one large fire.
bivy.notes: The best all-round camp on the Beverly Creek side, ringed by the peaks it serves — Iron Peak stands to the southwest, Teanaway Peak to the northwest, and the Bean and Earl ridges close it in to the southeast. It sits two and seven tenths miles up the Beverly Turnpike trail from the Beverly Creek trailhead. For Iron Peak it is the east-side option, which matters because the standard approach from the road end is entirely waterless: a party wanting to sleep out before the scramble is far better off here beside the creek than dry-camped on the saddle. It also links Earl Peak to Iron Peak over two days without returning to the car, and it is the staging point for the Fourth Creek crossing north to Ingalls Creek, which involves fording Ingalls Creek and is genuinely dangerous during June runoff. Ground is forested and level, insects are moderate, and the camp is low enough to be warm at night well into September.

bivy.name: Stafford Creek meadow camps below Navaho Pass
bivy.capacity: Established sites in the timber along the edge of a large meadow, with room for several parties; this is a popular long-weekend base camp and can hold a half dozen tents on a summer Saturday
bivy.water: The reason this camp exists. Stafford Creek and a side stream come down the rock faces at the meadow edge and run into late summer in most years, and this is the last dependable water before the pass. Above the meadow there is nothing: the final half mile of bare serpentine to Navaho Pass and the whole of the south slopes above it are completely dry, and on a hot east-side day that is four or five hours of climbing on what you carry.
bivy.permit: No permit, no quota, no lottery, and no connection to the Enchantment system. Northwest Forest Pass at the Stafford Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet here and the drainage is normally under a full burn ban by July. The Stafford Creek road and trail were inside the 2025 fire closure and were still subject to repair-work closures afterwards, so this is the site in the file most likely to be legally unreachable on any given date — check before you drive.
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Navaho Peak's south slopes and effectively the only one worth using on that side. From the Stafford Creek trailhead the trail climbs gently for the first mile beside the creek, then steepens as it pulls away from it, crosses a marshy open meadow, and reaches these camps at around five miles. Navaho Pass is another half mile up a bare serpentine slope at about 6,000 feet, and the south slopes above the pass are walking and easy scrambling to the summit. Most parties do the whole thing car to car and the camp is the contingency: a late start, a hot afternoon, or a group that wants the summit at dawn. It is also the hinge of the standard two-day loop that links Navaho Pass with the Bean Creek side and comes out at a different trailhead. The meadow is buggy in early summer and the burn scar in the drainage has changed shade and blowdown patterns, so expect the walking to be rougher than an older description suggests.

bivy.name: Lake Ann bench and the upper Esmeralda Basin camps
bivy.capacity: Small scattered sites rather than a campground — a bench part way up the Lake Ann branch takes a tent or two, and a knoll on its east side holds several more; nothing here suits a large group
bivy.water: The bench camp has running water beside it, fed by snowmelt draining the basin, and small streams cross the main basin trail lower down. All of it is snowmelt and all of it fades: reliable through July, marginal in August, and effectively gone by September, when the basin is dry rock and cured grass. There is no water at all on the pass or on either summit.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness above the basin, under the Cle Elum district and entirely outside the Enchantment Permit Area — a free self-issued slip from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use, with no quota, no lottery and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the Esmeralda Basin trailhead. No campfires; this is open subalpine meadow and the ban is both seasonal and permanent by elevation. Camping is prohibited at Ingalls Lake, which is a different basin over the divide, and the designated sites in Headlight Basin are the legal option on that side.
bivy.notes: The Esmeralda-side camp that is not Headlight Basin, and the one that actually serves the two peaks at the head of this valley. Esmeralda Peaks are scrambled directly from the basin on their standard route, and Fortune Peak's standard line goes up the basin and over the pass near Lake Ann before turning up the peak; both are honest day trips from the road end, so this is a place to sleep when the party is slow, the day is short, or you want two summits without driving twice. The trail leaves the road end at about 4,500 feet and climbs gently through meadow, timber and small stream crossings before the ground steepens toward the pass; take the Lake Ann branch to reach the bench and the knoll above it, which has a wide view back down the upper Teanaway. Fortune Peak can also be climbed by its east slope out of Headlight Basin, which is a different camp on the other side of the divide and is described with the Ingalls group rather than here. Mountain goats work this whole area and are bold about salt — keep gear packed and relieve yourself well away from camp.

bivy.name: Iron Peak saddle dry camp
bivy.capacity: A few flat spots at and just below the saddle between Iron Peak and Mount Teanaway; one or two small tents, no shelter, and nothing resembling an established site
bivy.water: None. This is the defining fact about the route and the camp both. The Iron Peak trail passes a steep unnamed creek in the first eighth of a mile from the trailhead and then turns away from it for good; you can hear water in the gullies on either side for half the climb and cannot reach any of it. Carry everything you intend to drink and cook with from the road, and plan on more than feels necessary, because this is a south-facing, sun-hammered hillside.
bivy.permit: No permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass at the Iron Peak trailhead. Campfires are prohibited at this elevation and there is nothing here to burn in any case. Pitch on gravel or bare ground; the saddle carries thin meadow that does not recover.
bivy.notes: A perch rather than a campsite, and included because Iron Peak's standard approach offers nothing else. The trailhead sits on the North Fork Teanaway Road roughly half a mile above the De Roux campground turn and a mile and a half short of the road end, at about 3,800 feet. The trail climbs a rib at a steady moderate grade with no flat ground and no water until it reaches the saddle, from which the scramble turns west up the ridge to the summit, and most parties continue on to Mount Teanaway from the same saddle. Almost nobody sleeps here and almost nobody needs to — this is a half-day objective for a fit party — but a group that has started late, or one linking Iron Peak with the Beverly Creek peaks over the divide, has this saddle as the only level ground on the route. It is windy, exposed and cold after dark even in August. If there is any choice at all, the creekside camps at the Fourth Creek junction on the other side of the divide are a far better place to spend a night.

bivy.name: Teanaway Community Forest campgrounds — 29 Pines, Teanaway Campground and Indian Camp
bivy.capacity: Large by the standards of this valley: roughly fifty-nine sites at 29 Pines, about fifty-five at the Teanaway camping area, and eleven plus two group sites at Indian Camp. All first come, first served, no reservations. Equestrian camping is confined to Indian Camp and the Teanaway camping area.
bivy.water: No potable water. Bring what you need or filter from the Teanaway River, which runs beside all three and is dependable year round at this elevation — a useful contrast with everything higher in the valley, which is snowmelt-fed and unreliable after July.
bivy.permit: This is state Community Forest land, not national forest, and the rules are genuinely different from the Forest Service ground further up the road. The campgrounds are free but a Discover Pass is required to park. Dispersed camping is PROHIBITED anywhere in the Community Forest — camping is confined to these designated campgrounds, and this is actively enforced, so the roadside pullout habit that works on the national forest above does not work down here. Stays are capped at seven days in any thirty. Rubbish is not collected, so everything packs out, and cutting firewood is not permitted. Fire restrictions arrive early and are strict.
bivy.notes: The low-valley drive-in option, on the paved and lower gravel stretches of the Teanaway River Road below the national forest boundary, and the practical answer for a party arriving late from the west side the night before a climb. It is a longer morning drive to the trailheads than the small Forest Service campgrounds higher up — 29 Pines sits at the point where the road turns to dirt, with the Stafford Creek fork about a mile beyond it, Beverly Creek several miles further and the Esmeralda road end roughly ten — but these have far more capacity, they are free, and they do not fill in the same way. The state ownership is the thing to internalise: the boundary between Community Forest rules and national forest rules falls partway up this road, camping law changes at it, and the change is not signed as clearly as it should be. Above the boundary the gravel road washboards badly by August, holds snow into early summer, and was subject to closure orders following the 2025 fire.

bivy.name: Bean Creek Basin meadows

bivy.permit: No permit and no quota. Nothing here is inside the Enchantment Permit Area and there is no lottery of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent annual pass is needed to park at the Beverly Creek trailhead. Where a trail from this basin crosses into the Alpine Lakes Wilderness further north, the free self-issue slip from the trailhead box covers it. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet in this national forest, which includes the basin, and the whole valley routinely falls under a total burn ban from midsummer onward. Camp on bare ground or duff, never on the meadow itself.
bivy.notes: This is the overnight base for Earl Peak, and it is a contingency rather than the plan — Earl is a straightforward day from the car for most parties, and the reason to sleep here is a late start, a slow party, or a wish to link Earl with Bean Peak and the surrounding scrambles over two days. From the Beverly Creek trailhead at about 3,600 feet, take the right-hand branch at the first junction half a mile in and climb steeply up the Bean Creek valley, crossing the creek to reach the basin at roughly two miles. From the basin the route continues to Earl Pass on the divide between Bean and Standup Creeks at about 6,200 feet, then turns north up the southwest ridge, which carries bits of boot tread most of the way and stays easy scrambling to the summit. The basin is a flower meadow in early July and dry gold by September; mosquitoes are bad from snowmelt through mid-July. The last mile and a half of road to the trailhead is a rough, overgrown one-lane track that punishes a low car.

bivy.capacity: A cluster of good sites near the creek holding four or five tents, spread over enough ground that two parties are not on top of each other
bivy.water: Beverly Creek runs briskly right beside the camp and is the most reliable water anywhere in this group of peaks. That reliability ends abruptly at the junction: the sites up on the saddle where the Fourth Creek and Hardscrabble trails meet are dry, and there is nothing on the climb to Iron Peak's saddle from this side. A small running source sits roughly four tenths of a mile down the Hardscrabble side of that saddle, off-trail, and is worth knowing about if you have committed to the high ground and misjudged.
bivy.permit: No permit, no quota, no lottery. Northwest Forest Pass at the Beverly Creek trailhead. The free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness slip from the trailhead box covers travel where the trails cross the boundary north of here. No campfires above 5,000 feet, and expect a valley-wide burn ban from midsummer; this is dry, brittle east-side timber that has already carried one large fire.
bivy.notes: The best all-round camp on the Beverly Creek side, ringed by the peaks it serves — Iron Peak stands to the southwest, Teanaway Peak to the northwest, and the Bean and Earl ridges close it in to the southeast. It sits two and seven tenths miles up the Beverly Turnpike trail from the Beverly Creek trailhead. For Iron Peak it is the east-side option, which matters because the standard approach from the road end is entirely waterless: a party wanting to sleep out before the scramble is far better off here beside the creek than dry-camped on the saddle. Ground is forested and level, insects are moderate, and the camp is low enough to be warm at night well into September.
